Here, we provide the detailed construction of the self-dual BB codes listed in Table 1 as well as the parallel magic state cultivation protocol for these codes.

Given a commutative quotient polynomial ring $R_{l,m}:=\mathbb{F}_{2}[x,y]/(x^{l}-1,y^{m}-1)$ and two polynomials $c,d\in R_{l,m}$ , a Bivariate Bicycle (BB) code $\mathrm{BB}(c,d;R_{l,m})$ is defined as a CSS code with check matrices [11]

$$ H_{X}=(c,d);\quad H_{Z}=(d^{T},c^{T}), $$

where $f^{T}$ for any polynomial $f\in R_{l,m}$ is defined by taking the inverse of each of its monomial terms.

As shown in Fig. 10(a), the physical qubits of a $\mathrm{BB}(c,d;R_{l,m})$ code can be arranged on two $l\times m$ blocks $U$ and $D$ , where each qubit $q(U,\alpha)$ or $q(R,\alpha)$ within the block $U$ or $D$ is labeled by the monomial $\alpha\in\mathcal{M}=\{x^{i}y^{j}\}_{i\in[l],j\in[m]}$ . Note that $R_{l,m}$ is equivalent to a vector space $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\mathcal{M}}$ with basis elements in $\mathcal{M}$ . Given a $f\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\mathcal{M}}$ , it can also be interpreted as a set in the powerset of $\mathcal{M}$ . Let $X(P,Q)$ (resp. $Z(P,Q))$ , where $P,Q\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\mathcal{M}}$ , denote a $X$ (resp. $Z$ ) Pauli operator supported on $\{q(U,\alpha)\}_{\alpha\in P}\cup\{q(D,\beta)\}_{\beta\in Q}$ .

In this work, we will focus on self-dual BB codes, which support transversal Hadamard and $S$ gates, by choosing odd $l$ and $m$ as well as polynomials that satisfy $d=c^{T}$ . In addition, by carefully choosing the polynomial $c$ , we identify codes with disjoint logical operators that can be translationally shifted on a toric layout by performing physical permutations. These choices result in the codes in Table 1 with weight- $8$ stabilizers and code parameters $[[n_{b}=2lm,k_{b}=2l,d_{b}\leq m]]$ . Below, we summarize the nontrivial features of these BB codes compared to the original ones in Ref. [11].

- 1. Transversal Clifford gates: The codes are self-dual and support transversal Hadamard and $S$ gates, i.e., $\overline{H}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ and $\overline{S}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ are implemented by $H^{\otimes n}$ and $S^{\otimes n}$ , respectively.

- 2. Disjoint logical support: We can find the following logical-operator basis: $\displaystyle\bar{X}_{U,i}$ $\displaystyle=X(x^{i}\chi,0),\quad\bar{Z}_{U,i}=Z(x^{i}\chi,0),$ (8) $\displaystyle\bar{X}_{D,i}$ $\displaystyle=X(0,x^{i}\chi),\quad\bar{Z}_{D,i}=Z(0,x^{i}\chi),$ where $\chi:=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}y^{j}$ , and $i$ iterates from $0$ to $l-1$ . As shown in Fig. 10, each logical qubit indexed by $i$ on the $U$ ( $D$ ) block has overlapped logical $X$ and $Z$ operators supported on the $i$ -th row of the $U$ ( $D$ ) block of the physical qubits.

- 3. Cyclic automorphisms: Logical qubits within each block can be cyclically permuted via automorphisms induced by shifts of the physical qubits, i.e., $(\bar{X}_{U,i},\bar{Z}_{U,i})\mapsto(\bar{X}_{U,(i+1)\bmod l},\bar{Z}_{U,(i+1)\bmod l})$ (and similarly for $D$ ) is implemented by $q(U,\alpha)\mapsto q(U,x\alpha)$ and $q(D,\alpha)\mapsto q(D,x\alpha)$ .

To prepare high-fidelity magic states for these BB codes, we first cultivate $\overline{\ket{T}}$ using small 2D color codes following the standard protocol in Ref. [27] and then transfer them into the BB codes using the following code-merging protocol.

The protocol utilizes the following subroutine for merging two quantum codes: Given two CSS codes $\mathcal{Q}_{A}$ and $\mathcal{Q_{B}}$ with logical operators $(\bar{X}_{A},\bar{Z}_{A})$ and $(\bar{X}_{B},\bar{Z}_{B})$ (we focus on one particular logical qubit for ease of presentation”), respectively, we could use an adapter $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{A-B}}$ to merge the two codes by performing a joint logical measurement $\bar{X}_{A}\bar{X}_{B}$ . Starting from the code $\mathcal{Q}_{A}$ and initializing the data qubits of $\mathcal{Q}_{B}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{A-B}}$ in the product $\ket{0}$ states, we can also view this procedure as growing the code from $\mathcal{Q}_{A}$ to the merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{AB}$ with a logical $X$ operator $\bar{X}_{A}$ and a grown logical $Z$ operator $\bar{Z}_{A}\bar{Z}_{B}$ . Thus, this merging protocol grows the $Z$ distance of the code (rigorously proved in Supplement Note V) utilizing the adapter that enables a joint $\bar{X}_{A}\bar{X}_{B}$ logical measurement. We refer to the above protocol as an $X$ -merging protocol with a $X$ -type adapter. We can similarly construct a $Z$ -merging protocol with a $Z$ -type adapter, which enables a joint $\bar{Z}_{A}\bar{Z}_{B}$ measurement, growing the $X$ distance of the code.

For a BB code encoding $k_{b}$ logical qubits, starting from $k_{b}$ copies of $[[n_{c},1,d_{c}]]$ color codes $\mathcal{Q}_{C}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ , we first grow the $X$ distance of the codes by merging $\mathcal{Q}_{C}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ with $k_{b}$ copies of $[[n_{s},1,d_{s,X},d_{s,Z}=d_{c}]]$ thin surface codes $\mathcal{Q}_{S}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ through $k_{b}$ $Z$ -type adapters (see the purple strip in Fig. 10). The $k_{b}$ copies of the merged color-surface code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ then have a $Z$ distance $d_{c}$ and a $X$ distance $d_{c}+d_{s,X}$ . Next, we grow the $Z$ distance of the code by merging $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ with a $[[n_{b},k_{b},d_{b}]]$ BB code through a $X$ -type adapter $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}$ that consists of $k_{b}$ disjoint and identical adapters $\{\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{k_{b}}$ , each coupling the $i$ -th logical qubit of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ to a copy of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ (see the orange strip in Fig. 10 for $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ ). By choosing $d_{c}+d_{s,X}\sim d_{b}$ , we obtain a merged color-surface-BB code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ that encodes $k_{b}$ logical qubits with a distance $\sim d_{b}$ (see Supplement Note V). The above two-step merging protocol, analogous to the grafting procedure from a color code to a surface code [27], then transfers the magic states cultivated in the $k$ color codes to the merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ .

To maintain the low space overhead of the BB code, we use small color codes with $d_{c}\ll d_{b}$ . In this regime, post-selection (error detection) must be applied before the code reaches full distance $d_{b}$ to avoid degrading the logical error rate, which could potentially reduce the overall success probability. Fortunately, aided by the thin surface codes, our protocol rapidly grows the code distance to $d_{b}$ . Moreover, by restricting post-selection to small spatial regions centered on the color codes, we achieve low logical error rates while maintaining high success probabilities. See Supplementary Note V for details.

As a concrete example, we can merge $6$ copies of $[[7,1,3]]$ color codes with a $[[66,6,8]]$ -BB code with $6$ copies of $[[12,1,d_{s,X}=4,d_{s,Z}=3]]$ thin surface codes, resulting in a $[[324,6,7]]$ merged color-surface-BB code. See Supplement Note V for details.

### VII.7 Fault-tolerant compilation

Here, we formalize the fault-tolerant compilation problem using our batched high-rate logical gadgets $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ and analyze the compilation overhead in detail.

Considzer a Clifford + $T$ circuit on $K$ qubits, $C=\prod_{t=1}^{D_{P}}C_{t}$ , where each layer $C_{t}$ of the circuit is drawn from the gate set $\mathbf{B}_{P}$ , which consists of $\{$ arbitrary $K$ -qubit Hadamard gates $\}$ $\cup$ $\{$ arbitrary $K$ -qubit $S$ gates $\}$ $\cup$ $\{$ arbitrary non-overlapping CNOTs on $K$ -qubits $\}$ $\cup$ $\{$ arbitrary $K$ -qubit $T$ gates $\}$ . Note that $\mathbf{B}_{P}$ are essentially all possible parallel gates of the same type that are implementable with physical qubits under long-range connectivity. Note that any conventional Clifford + T circuit can be turned into the above form with a constant overhead 33 3 According to Ref. [83], any Clifford circuit can be decomposed into a canonical form of 11 blocks, each consisting of only one type of gates from gate set $\{\mathrm{CNOT},S,H\}$ . In addition, as detailed in Sec. VII.4, each layer of addressable $T$ gates can be implemented by a layer of global $T$ gates and a constant number of layers of addressable Clifford operations. We aim to analyze the overhead of further compiling each layer $C_{t}$ into our batched gate set $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ in depth $D_{\mathbf{B}_{L}}(C_{t})$ , i.e. $C_{t}=\prod_{t^{\prime}=1}^{D_{\mathbf{B}_{L}}(C_{t})}C_{t,t^{\prime}}$ , where each $C_{t,t^{\prime}}$ is drawn from $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ . We simply refer to the extra overhead for compiling $C$ , $\left[\sum_{t=1}^{D_{P}}D_{\mathbf{B}_{L}}(C_{t})\right]/D_{P}$ , as the compilation overhead.

For concreteness, we specify our batched gate set $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ here. We distribute the total of $K$ logical qubits into $K/k_{1}$ blocks of $[[n_{1},k_{1},d_{1}]]$ $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ codes. Here, we assume that $K/k_{1}$ is larger than the batch size for the BAC gadget, i.e. $K=\Omega(d_{1}^{2})$ . Let $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{BC}}$ denote the set of depth- $1$ physical Clifford gates that are implementable by a single BAC gadget in Theorem 3, which takes the following form: take any depth- $1$ Clifford circuit $C_{1}$ on $k_{1}$ qubits and assign it to an arbitrary subset of $k^{\prime}\leq K/k_{1}$ $Q_{1}$ blocks (the rest being applied with identity) 44 4 Note that when $K/k_{1}$ is much lager than the batch size $\mathcal{O}(d_{1}^{2})$ of a BAC gadget, we can have multiple batches implementing distinct $k_{1}$ -qubit circuits, which are beyond the operations in the current $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{BC}}$ . We neglect such a flexibility for now.. Let $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{GT}}=\{\bar{T}^{\otimes K}\}$ be the global $T$ gates. We thus take the logical gadget basis as $\mathbf{B}_{L}=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{BC}}\cup\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{GT}}$ .

We note that the compilation overhead is not equivalent to the time overhead of fault-tolerantly implementing a circuit as the global $T$ gates in $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ are not implemented using a constant-depth physical circuit. Rather, it characterizes the extra time overhead that arises from the limited addressability/parallelism of the gadgets in $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ (compared to $\mathbf{B}_{P}$ ) on top of the time overhead of the gadgets themselves in $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ .

#### VII.7.1 Worst-case compilation overhead

We show that the worst-case compilation overhead defined above using our batched gadgets $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ scales at least linearly with $k_{1}$ , the number of logical qubits per qLDPC block $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ .

Specifically, we construct a $K$ -qubit CNOT circuit $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}$ —comprising only CNOT gates—that can be implemented with physical depth $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K)$ , yet requires logical depth at least $\tilde{\Omega}(Kk_{1})$ when compiled using $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ .

As shown in Ref. [79], any CNOT circuit $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}$ can be decomposed into layers of non-overlapping CNOT gates within $\mathbf{B}_{P}$ , yielding a physical depth

$$ D_{\mathbf{B}_{P}}(C_{\mathrm{CNOT}})=\mathcal{O}(K/\log K). $$

To lower bound the corresponding logical depth $D_{\mathbf{B}_{L}}(C_{\mathrm{CNOT}})$ , we analyze the size of $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ and apply a simple counting argument.

#### Lemma 8 (Size of the batched gadgets $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ ).

Given $K$ logical qubits distributed in $K/k_{1}$ blocks of a $[[n_{1},k_{1},d_{1}]]$ CSS qLDPC code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ , where $K=\Omega(k_{1}^{2})$ , the batched gadgets have a size

$$ |\mathbf{B}_{L}|=\exp[\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K/k_{1})]. $$

#### Proof.

Recall that the batched gadgets consist of batched $H$ gates, batched $S$ gates, batched CNOT gates, and global $T$ gates. The size $|\mathbf{B}_{L}|$ is dominated by the number of distinct batched CNOT gates. Let $\mathbf{S}_{2}=\{\{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\}\}_{i}$ be a two-block partition of the indices of the $K/k_{1}$ blocks, $[K/k_{1}]$ , i.e. $\{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\}$ and $\{\alpha_{j},\beta_{j}\}$ are two distinct pairs for $i\neq j$ and $\bigcup_{i}\{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\}=[K/k_{1}]$ . A BAC gadget can apply any $2k_{1}$ -qubit CNOT circuit of a physical depth $1$ to any subset of the pairs of the blocks in $\mathbf{S}_{2}$ . Denote the set of all two-block partitions of $[K/k_{1}]$ as $\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{2}(K/k_{1})$ and the set of all depth- $1$ $2k_{1}$ -qubit CNOT circuits as $\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{CNOT,P}}(2k_{1})$ . The size of all distinct batched CNOTs is then given by

$$ |\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{2}(K/k_{1})|\times|\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{CNOT,P}}(2k_{1})|\times 2^{K/(2k_{1})}, $$

where the contribution $2^{K/(2k_{1})}$ comes from the fact that for each of the $K/(2k_{1})$ pairs of blocks, we can decide whether or not to apply the selected $2k_{1}$ -qubit CNOT circuit. Following a simple combinatorial analysis, we have $|\bm{\mathcal{S}}_{2}(K/k_{1})|=(K/k_{1})!/[K/(2k_{1})]!=\exp{\tilde{\Theta}(K/k_1)}$ . According to Ref. [79], we have $|\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{CNOT}}(2k_{1})|=\exp{\tilde{\Theta}(k_1)}$ . In the regime where $K=\Omega(k_{1}^{2})$ (there are more than $\Theta(k_{1})$ $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ blocks), we then have $|\mathbf{B}_{L}|=\exp{\tilde{\mc{O}}(K/k_1)}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 9 (Worst-case compilation overhead of the batched gadgets).

There exists a $K$ -qubit CNOT circuit $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}$ with

$$ D_{\mathbf{B}_{L}}(C_{\mathrm{CNOT}})/D_{\mathbf{B}_{P}}(C_{\mathrm{CNOT}})=\tilde{\Omega}(k_{1}), $$

#### Proof.

According to Ref. [79], the number of distinct $K$ -qubit CNOT circuits is $|\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{CNOT}}(K)|=\exp\{\tilde{\Theta}(K^{2})\}$ , Whereas, according to Lemma. 10, the number of distinct gates in each layer of batched gadgets is $|\mathbf{B}_{L}|=\exp{\tilde{O}(K/k_1)}$ . Therefore, it takes a minimal logical depth of

$$ D^{*}=\log{|\mb{C}_{\mr{CNOT}}(K)|}/\log{|\mb{B}_L|}=\tilde{\Omega}(Kk_{1}), $$

to reach all possible $K$ -qubit CNOTs. This indicates that there exists at least one $K$ -qubit CNOT $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}\in\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{CNOT}}(K)$ such that the logical depth $D_{\mathbf{B}_{L}}(C_{\mathrm{CNOT}})=\tilde{\Omega}(Kk_{1})$ . In contrast, the physical depth is always $D_{\mathbf{B}_{P}}(C_{\mathrm{CNOT}})=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(K)$ [79]. This leads to the compilation overhead $\tilde{\Omega}(k_{1})$ in Eq. (12). ∎

#### VII.7.2 Batched compilation

Now, we present a concrete compilation scheme with the batched gadgets $\mathbf{B}_{L}$ .

Given $K$ qubits in $K/k_{1}$ $k_{1}$ -qubit blocks, we can partition them into multiple sectors, each composed of several $k_{1}$ -qubit blocks. Specifically, we define a partition $\mathbf{S}=\{S_{i}\}$ of the set of the block indices $[K/k_{1}]$ , where each $S_{i}\subseteq[K/k_{1}]$ and $[K/k_{1}]=\bigcup_{i}S_{i}$ .

If a $K$ -qubit circuit $C$ can be written as a tensor product over the sectors,

$$ C=\bigotimes_{S_{i}\in\mathbf{S}}C_{S_{i}}, $$

where each $C_{S_{i}}$ is a $(|S_{i}|\times k_{1})$ -qubit circuit supported only on the blocks indexed by $S_{i}$ , we denote the sector-wise decomposition of $C$ as

$$ (C)_{\mathbf{S}}:=\{C_{S_{i}}\}_{S_{i}\in\mathbf{S}}. $$

As an example, consider a $K$ -qubit Hadamard circuit $C_{H}$ . Its decomposition into a collection of $k_{1}$ -qubit Hadamard circuits acting on each $k_{1}$ -qubit block individually corresponds to the partition $[[K/k_{1}]]:=\{\{i\}\}_{i\in[K/k_{1}]}$ , so we write the decomposition as $(C_{H})_{[[K/k_{1}]]}$ .

Now, we describe a compilation scheme whose overhead for a given circuit $C$ is related to the property of the distribution of the sectors that $C$ is partitioned into.

We first compile $C$ into layers of physical circuits consisting of only local $H$ , $S$ , CNOT, or global $T$ gates, i.e. $C=\prod_{t=1}^{D_{\mathbf{B}_{P}}(C)}C_{t}$ , where each $C_{t}$ consists exclusively of either $H$ gates, $S$ gates, non-overlapping CNOTs, or global $T$ gates $T^{\otimes K}$ . Then, we further compile each circuit layer $C_{t}$ using the batched gadgets. A layer of global $T$ gates can be implemented using simply a batched $T$ gadget. It thus remains to compile circuit layers of type $H$ , $S$ , or CNOT.

We first consider a circuit layer of $H$ gates, $C_{H}$ , and the compilation for a layer of $S$ gates is analogous. Choosing a single-block partition $[[K/k_{1}]]$ , $C_{H}$ can be partitioned into $K/k_{1}$ $k_{1}$ -qubit sectors $(C_{H})_{[[K/k_{1}]]}$ . We say that a set of generators $\mathbf{G}=\{g_{j}\}_{j=1}^{|\mathbf{G}|}$ , where $g_{i}$ is a $k_{1}$ -qubit $H$ circuit, generate $(C_{H})_{[[K/k_{1}]]}$ if

$$ C_{i}=\prod_{j=1}^{|\mathbf{G}|}g_{j}^{a_{i,j}}, $$

for any $C_{i}\in(C_{H})_{[[K/k_{1}]]}$ , where $a_{i,j}\in\{0,1\}$ . As an example, $\mathbf{G}_{H}:=\{H_{i}\otimes I^{\otimes(k_{1}-1)}\}_{i\in[k_{1}]}$ with $|\mathbf{G}_{H}|=k_{1}$ , where $H_{i}\otimes I^{\otimes(k_{1}-1)}$ denotes a circuit that applies a Hadamard gate on the $i$ -th qubit and identity on the remaining $k_{1}-1$ qubits, generates any collection of $k_{1}$ -qubit Hadamard circuits.

Given such a generating set $\mathbf{G}$ , an elementary BAC gadget in Theorem 3 can naturally implement a generator element in $\mathbf{G}$ on any subset of the $K/k_{1}$ blocks in one logical step and execute the full circuit layer $C_{H}$ by implementing $\mathbf{G}$ sequentially:

$$ C_{H}=\prod_{j=1}^{|\mathbf{G}|}\bigotimes_{i=1}^{K/k_{1}}(g_{j}^{a_{i,j}}). $$

Choosing a minimal generating set $\mathbf{G}$ minimizes the compilation depth $|\mathbf{G}|$ for $C_{H}$ . Note that here we assume a large batch size of $K/k_{1}$ , i.e. the same gate (or identity) is applied to all the $K/k_{1}$ blocks at a given time step, which results in the strictly sequential implementation of $\mathbf{G}$ . More efficient compilation is possible by using a smaller batch size, as long as it satisfies the batching constraints from the construction of the batched logical gadgets.

Next, we consider a circuit layer of CNOTs, $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}$ . We first decompose it as an intra-block CNOT circuit $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{intra}}$ and an inter-block CNOT circuit $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{inter}}$

$$ C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}=C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{inter}}C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{intra}}, $$

where $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{inter}}$ (resp. $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{intra}}$ ) only consists of CNOTs across (resp. within) different $k_{1}$ -qubit blocks. To implement $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{intra}}$ , we can again simply choose the one-block partition $\mathbf{S}=[[K/k_{1}]]$ and implement a minimal generating set $\mathbf{G}$ of $(C_{\mathrm{CNOT}})_{[[K/k_{1}]]}$ sequentially, in a depth $|\mathbf{G}|$ analogous to Eq. (16).

To implement $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{inter}}$ , we partition it into certain two-block circuits, i.e. choosing $\mathbf{S}$ in the form of $\{\{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\}\}_{i}$ , in the following. We define a graph $G(\mathbf{V},\mathbf{E})$ , where the vertices $\mathbf{V}$ are associated with the $k_{1}$ blocks and each physical CNOT in $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{inter}}$ is associated with an edge $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbf{E}$ if it is supported on two qubits in the $\alpha$ -th and the $\beta$ -th block, respectively. An edge-coloration $\mathbf{E}=\bigcup_{c\in\mathbf{c}}\mathbf{E}_{c}$ gives a decomposition of $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{inter}}$ into $|\mathbf{c}|$ layers of CNOTs, $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{inter}}=\prod_{c\in\bm{\vec{c}}}C_{c}$ , where $C_{c}$ has a partition into two-block CNOTs according to $\mathbf{E}_{c}$ , $(C_{c})_{\mathbf{E}_{c}}$ .

Then, we implement the $|\mathbf{c}|$ layers of the two-block CNOTs $\{C_{c}\}_{c\in\mathbf{c}}$ sequentially using the batched logical gadgets. For each layer $C_{c}$ , we again implement a minimal generating set $\mathbf{G}$ of its two-block partition $(C_{c})_{\mathbf{E}_{c}}$ sequentially, analogous to Eq. (16). Note that the minimum compilation depth of $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\mathrm{inter}}$ is obtained by minimizing over the choice of the coloration and the corresponding generating set.

Supplementary Information for “Batched high-rate logical operations for quantum LDPC codes”

## S1 Batched Syndrome Extraction

Here, we present the detailed construction of the batched syndrome extraction (BSE) gadget and prove its fault tolerance (see Theorem 14, the formal version of the Theorem 1 in the main text).

We first introduce some helpful notations and definitions in Sec. S1.1. We then detail the BSE construction in Sec. S1.2 and put together a formal description of the logical action of the BSE gadget (Prop. 13) as well as its fault tolerance (Theorem 14). Then, in Sec. S1.3, we prove the fault tolerance Theorem 14. In Sec. S1.4, we draw connections between our BSE gadget and the cluster-state scheme in Ref. [32]. Finally, in Sec. S1.6, we provide the details of the numerical simulation of the BSE gadget presented in the main text.

### S1.1 Notations and definitions

Given a vector $f\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ , we denote $\mathrm{supp}(f)\subseteq[n]$ as its support. Given another matrix $M\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times n}$ , we denote $[f]_{M}:=\{f^{\prime}\mid Mf^{\prime}=Mf\}$ as the equivalent class of $f$ with respect to $M$ . Furthermore, we denote $|f|^{r}_{M}:=\min_{f^{\prime}\in[f]_{M}}|f^{\prime}|$ as the reduced weight of $f$ with respect to $M$ .

We denote $e^{n}_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ as a unit vector with the $i$ -th entry being $1$ .

#### Definition 10 (Left-expanding graph).

Let $G=(A\cup B,E)$ be a bipartite regular graph with degree- $\Delta_{A}$ vertices $A$ and degree- $\Delta_{B}$ vertices $B$ . We say that $G$ is $(\gamma_{A},\delta_{A})$ -left-expanding if for any $S\subseteq A$ with $|S|\leq\gamma_{A}|A|$ , we have

$$ |\Gamma(S)|\geq(1-\delta_{A})\Delta_{A}|S|, $$

where $\Gamma(S)\subseteq B$ denotes the neighbor of $S$ .

#### Definition 11 (Expander Code).

A classical code $C$ with check matrix $H_{C}$ is $(\gamma,\delta)$ -expanding if the bipartite Tanner graph $G=(A\cup B,E)$ defined from $H_{C}$ , where $A$ and $B$ represent the bits and the checks of $H_{C}$ , respectively, is $(\gamma,\delta)$ -left expanding.

#### Definition 12 (Locally stochastic noise).

A distribution $\mathrm{Pr}(e)$ of a random vector $e$ is locally stochastic if there exists some constant $p$ such that

$$ \tilde{\mathrm{Pr}}(e):=\sum_{\mathrm{supp}(e^{\prime})\supseteq\mathrm{supp}(e)}\mathrm{Pr}(e^{\prime})\leq p^{|e|}. $$

### S1.2 Construction of the BSE gadget

*Figure 11: Illustration of the proof for BSE. The stars represent the four types of phenomenological syndrome or data errors that we consider during the protocol, which are detailed in the texts.*

Here, we present a detailed construction of the BSE gadget.

Given a $[n_{C},k_{C},d_{C}]$ classical LDPC code with a check matrix $H_{C}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{C}\times n_{C}}$ , where $\sigma_{C}=n_{C}-k_{C}$ . Up to permutation of the bits, we assume that $H_{C}$ is in its canonical form with a conjugate generator matrix $G_{C}=(I_{k_{C}},P)$ , where $P\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k_{C}\times(n_{C}-k_{C})}$ , with $H_{C}G_{C}^{T}=0\mod 2$ . We measure the $X$ checks of a $[[n,k,d]]$ CSS qLDPC code $\mathcal{Q}$ with $X$ checks $H_{X}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{X}\times n}$ and $Z$ checks $H_{Z}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{Z}\times n}$ using the following protocol:

- 1. Input: $k_{C}$ $\mathcal{Q}$ blocks. Denote this set of blocks $\bm{B}_{0}$ . Start by measuring the $X$ checks of $\mathcal{Q}^{\otimes k_{C}}$ in $\bm{B}_{0}$ once.

- 2. Initialize $\sigma_{C}$ ancilla blocks in $|0\rangle^{\otimes n}$ , and measure the $X$ checks of $\mathcal{Q}^{\otimes\sigma_{C}}$ once. Denote this set of blocks $\bm{B}_{1}$ .

- 3. Initialize $\sigma_{C}$ ancilla blocks in $|+\rangle^{\otimes n}$ , and measure the $Z$ checks of $\mathcal{Q}^{\otimes\sigma_{C}}$ once. Denote this set of blocks $\bm{A}$ .

- 4. Apply $\bm{A}$ -controlled transversal CNOTs targeting $\bm{B}_{0}$ and $\bm{B}_{1}$ based on $H_{C}$ : Let the blocks of $\bm{B}_{0}\cup\bm{B}_{1}$ be indexed by $[n_{C}]$ and the blocks of $\bm{A}$ indexed by $[\sigma_{C}]$ . Apply a transversal CNOT between the $i$ -th block of $\bm{A}$ and the $j$ -th block of $\bm{B}_{0}\cup\bm{B}_{1}$ if $H_{C}[i,j]=1$ .

- 5. Measure transversely blocks in $\bm{B}_{1}$ in the $Z$ basis and blocks in $\bm{A}$ in the $X$ -basis.

- 6. Perform error correction using detectors in the circuits (described in the following) and apply a feedback Pauli $X$ correction on $\bm{B}_{0}$ based on the $Z$ measurement outcomes of $\bm{B}_{1}$ as follows: apply a classically-controlled transversal CNOT from the $j$ -th block of $\bm{B}_{1}$ to the $i$ -th block of $\bm{B}_{0}$ if $P_{ij}=1$ .

See Fig. 11 for an illustration of the protocol.

We establish the following notation for describing qubits and checks of $m$ blocks of $\mathcal{Q}$ , $\mathcal{Q}^{\otimes m}$ : Let $e^{m}_{i}\otimes e^{n}_{j}$ be a basis vector associated with the $j$ -th qubit of the $i$ -th $\mathcal{Q}$ block, and similarly, $e^{m}_{i}\otimes e^{\sigma_{X}}_{j}$ ( $e^{m}_{i}\otimes e^{\sigma_{Z}}_{j}$ ) be a basis vector associated with the $j$ -th $X$ ( $Z$ ) check of the $i$ -th $\mathcal{Q}$ block. The space of $mn$ -qubit Pauli $X$ (or $Z$ ) operators are then spanned by $\{e^{m}_{i}\otimes e^{n}_{j}\}_{i\in[m],j\in[n]}$ . Correspondingly, the $X$ ( $Z$ ) check matrix of $\mathcal{Q}^{\otimes m}$ is given by $I_{m}\otimes H_{X}$ ( $I_{m}\otimes H_{Z}$ ). Similarly, a vector indexing a subset of $X$ ( $Z$ ) checks of $\mathcal{Q}^{\otimes m}$ is in $\langle e^{m}_{i}\otimes e^{\sigma_{X}}_{j}\rangle_{i\in[m],j\in[\sigma_{X}]}$ ( $\langle e^{m}_{i}\otimes e^{\sigma_{X}}_{j}\rangle_{i\in[m],j\in[\sigma_{Z}]}$ ).

We first show that in the absence of errors within the BSE gadget, the protocol is equivalent to only measuring a round of $X$ checks for $\bm{B}_{0}$ .

#### Proposition 13 (Action of the BSE gadget in the absence of errors).

In the absence of errors during the BSE gadget, the six-step protocol above is equivalent to measuring the $X$ checks of $\bm{B}_{0}$ once.

#### Proof.

Measuring the $X$ checks of $\bm{B}_{0}$ once projects $\bm{B}_{0}$ into eigenstates of $I_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{X}$ , which will be superposition of eigenstates of the $Z$ checks and logicals of $\bm{B}_{0}$ , i.e. $\{I_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{Z},I_{k_{C}}\otimes L_{Z}\}$ , where $L_{Z}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k\times n}$ denotes the $Z$ logical matrix of $\mathcal{Q}$ . Since the circuit of the BSE gadget commutes with $I_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{X}$ , it remains to prove that any state that is also an eigenstate of $\{I_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{Z},I_{k_{C}}\otimes L_{Z}\}$ remains the same after the BSE gadget. It suffices to show this by checking it for the $+1$ eigenstates of $\{I_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{Z},I_{k_{C}}\otimes L_{Z}\}$ . In this case, $\bm{B}_{0}$ is initially stabilized by $\{I_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{Z},I_{k_{C}}\otimes L_{Z}\}$ and we aim to show that it remains so at the output of the BSE gadget. We prove this by checking the transformation of $\{I_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{Z},I_{k_{C}}\otimes L_{Z}\}$ throughout the circuit.

It is easy to see that after step 2, the blocks $\bm{B}_{0}$ and $\bm{B}_{1}$ are stabilized by $\{I_{n_{C}}\otimes H_{Z},I_{n_{C}}\otimes L_{Z}\}$ . Next, the transversal $X$ measurements of $\bm{A}$ contains the measurements of the $X$ operators $\{H_{C}\otimes H_{X},H_{C}\otimes L_{X}\}$ on $\bm{B}_{0}\cup\bm{B}_{1}$ . This transforms the $Z$ -type stabilizers to $\{I_{n_{C}}\otimes H_{Z},G_{C}\otimes L_{Z}\}$ . Note that the $Z$ logical operators have delocalized across the $n_{C}$ blocks. The final transversal measurements on $\bm{B}_{1}$ then projects the system into an eigenstate of $\{I_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{Z},I_{k_{C}}\otimes L_{Z}\}$ , with the $Z$ checks $I_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{Z}$ having eigenvalues $+1$ . However, $I_{k_{C}}\otimes L_{Z}$ might have random eigenvalues. This is finally fixed by the Pauli $X$ feedback in step 4, which ensures the eigenvalues of $I_{k_{C}}\otimes L_{Z}$ get back to $+1$ . ∎

Now, we analyze the fault tolerance of the BSE gadget by considering a phenomenological noise model that contains the following four sets of errors $\mathcal{E}=\{e^{Z}_{d},e^{Z}_{s},e^{X}_{d},e^{X}_{s}\}$ :

- 1. $e^{Z}_{d}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{C}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ : $Z$ data error on $\bm{A}$ before the final transversal $X$ measurements.

- 2. $e^{Z}_{s}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n_{C}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{X}}$ : syndrome error on the initial measurements of the $X$ checks of $\bm{B}_{0}\cup\bm{B}_{1}$ .

- 3. $e^{X}_{d}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{C}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ : $X$ data error on $\bm{B}_{1}$ before the final $Z$ transversal measurements.

- 4. $e^{X}_{s}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{C}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{Z}}$ : syndrome error on the initial measurements of the $Z$ checks of $\bm{A}$ .

See the blue and green stars in Fig. 11 for an illustration of these errors. We consider that these errors $\mathcal{E}$ are locally stochastic (see Def. 19) with the same physical error rate $p$ . The fault tolerance of the BSE gadget can be fully captured by its tolerance against $\mathcal{E}$ since all locally stochastic errors at other locations are equivalent to the combination of $\mathcal{E}$ and/or some locally stochastic residual errors at the output.

Now, we describe the detectors for correcting $\mathcal{E}$ . By assumption, $H_{C}$ is in the following canonical form: $H_{C}=(H_{C}^{0},H_{C}^{1})$ , where $H_{C}^{0}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{C}\times k_{C}}$ represents the first $k_{C}$ columns of $H_{C}$ and $H_{C}^{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{C}\times\sigma_{C}}$ , being full rank, represents the last $\sigma_{C}$ columns of $H_{C}$ .

The $X$ detectors for correcting a $Z$ -type error $e^{Z}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}e^{Z}_{d}\\ e^{Z}_{s}\end{array}\right)$ are described by a $X$ detector matrix

$$ D_{X}=\left(I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{X},H_{C}\otimes I_{\sigma_{X}}\right), $$

and the $Z$ detectors for correcting a $X$ -type error $e^{X}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}e^{X}_{d}\\ e^{X}_{s}\end{array}\right)$ are given by a $Z$ detector matrix

$$ D_{Z}=\left(I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z},(H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{\sigma_{Z}}\right). $$

See Fig. 11 for an illustration of these detectors.

After performing error correction using the $X$ and $Z$ detectors, there will be two types of residual errors on the output $\bm{B}_{0}$ block:

- 1. $r_{s}^{Z}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k_{C}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{X}}$ :residual syndrome error on the initial measurements of the $X$ checks of $\bm{B}_{0}$ .

- 2. $r^{X}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k_{C}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ : residual $X$ data error on $\mathbf{B}_{0}$ .

Note that the residual $Z$ data errors will simply be the initial $Z$ errors on the $\bm{B}_{0}$ commuting through the circuit, therefore being locally stochastic automatically.

The fault tolerance of the BSE gadget in the presence of $\mathcal{E}$ is formally stated in the following theorem:

#### Theorem 14 (Formal statement of Theorem 1 in the main text).

If $H_{C}=(H_{C}^{0},H_{C}^{1})$ satisfies the following condition

- 1. $H_{C}^{1}$ is full rank.

- 2. $H_{C}$ is $(\gamma,\delta)$ -expanding for some constants $\gamma$ and $\delta<1/4$ (see Def. 11).

- 3. $(H_{C}^{1})^{T}$ is $(\gamma^{\prime},\delta^{\prime})$ -expanding for some constants $\gamma^{\prime}$ and $\delta^{\prime}<1/4$ .

- 4. $H_{C}$ is LDPC and $d_{C}=\Omega(d)$ .

Then, after applying minimum-weight corrections based on the circuit detectors, in the limit $d\rightarrow\infty$ and provided that the physical error rate $p$ is below some constant threshold, the residual $X$ syndrome error $r^{Z}_{s}$ and the residual $X$ data error $r^{X}$ satisfy:

- 1. $r^{Z}_{s}$ is the boundary of some locally stochastic $Z$ data error on $\mathbf{B}_{0}$ , i.e., there exists $h^{Z}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k_{C}\otimes n}$ such that

$$ \mathrm{Pr}(r^{Z}_{s}=(I_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{X})h^{Z})\leq\mathcal{O}(p)^{|h^{Z}|}, $$

(22)

- 2. $r^{X}$ is locally stochastic.

### S1.3 Proof of BSE Theorem 14

We sketch the main ideas behind the proof here. For both the $Z$ - and $X$ -type errors, we aim to show that some effective residual data error $h$ (e.g. $h^{Z}$ in Eq. (22)) is locally stochastic after error correction using the BSE detectors Eqs. (20)(21). This residual error $h$ is caused by some locally stochastic circuit fault $f$ . Analogous to the proof for single-shot QEC assuming confinement or soundness [23, 36], we first show that the weight of the $h$ can be upper-bounded by the weight of $f$ , indicating that small faults would only produce small residual errors. This utilizes the structure of the detectors matrices Eqs. (20)(21) as the check matrices of some HGP code and a “soundness” lemma (Lemma 21) for a HGP code with one expanding base code. Then, combining with some variants of the cluster-counting techniques from Ref. [1] (Lemma. 17), which upper-bound the number of circuit faults that lead to the same residual error $h$ , we can prove the local stochastic property of $r^{Z}_{s}$ and $r^{X}$ in Sec. S1.3.2 and Sec. S1.3.3, respectively. Finally, we present a family of classical codes that satisfy the requirements in Theorem 14 via random constructions [84, 34].

#### S1.3.1 Important mathematical lemmas

We first establish two key mathematical lemmas that facilitate our proof: Lemma 17 that bounds the probability of an equivalent class $[e]_{M}$ with respect to a LDPC matrix $M$ when $e$ is locally stochastic; Lemma 21 that relates the syndrome weight of a HGP code with its data error weight when the base classical codes are sufficiently expanding.

#### Lemma 15 (Lemma 2 of Ref. [1]).

Let $G=(\mathbf{V},\mathbf{E})$ be a graph with bounded degree $z$ , and $\mathbf{S}\subseteq\mathbf{V}$ be a subset of vertices. Let $M_{z}(s,\mathbf{S})$ be the number of size- $s$ sets containing $\mathbf{S}$ (i.e., with $s-|\mathbf{S}|$ extra nodes beyond those in $\mathbf{S}$ ), and which are a union of connected clusters, each of which contains a node in $\mathbf{S}$ . Then

$$ M_{z}(s,\mathbf{S})\leq e^{|\mathbf{S}|-1}(ze)^{s-|\mathbf{S}|}. $$

#### Corollary 16.

Let $G=(\mathbf{V},\mathbf{E})$ be a graph with bounded degree $z$ , and $\mathbf{S}\subseteq\mathbf{V}$ be a subset of vertices. Let $M^{\prime}_{z}(s,\mathbf{S})$ be the number of size- $s$ sets that are a union of connected clusters each containing at least one vertex in $\mathbf{S}$ . Then

$$ M^{\prime}_{z}(s,\mathbf{S})\leq\frac{(ze)^{s}}{e}[(1+\frac{1}{z})^{|\mathbf{S}|}-1]. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\mathbf{M}(s,\mathbf{S})$ be the collection of size- $s$ sets that contain $\mathbf{S}$ and are a union of connected clusters each containing at least one vertex in $\mathcal{S}$ , $\mathbf{M}^{\prime}(s,\mathbf{S})$ be the collection of size- $s$ sets that are a union of connected clusters each containing at least one vertex in $S$ . Then,

$$ \mathbf{M}^{\prime}(s,\mathbf{S})\subseteq\bigcup_{\mathbf{S}_{0}\subseteq\mathbf{S}}\mathbf{M}(s,\mathbf{S}_{0}). $$

Therefore,

$$ M^{\prime}_{z}(s,S)=|\mathbf{M}^{\prime}(s,\mathbf{S})|\leq\sum_{\mathbf{S}_{0}\subseteq\mathbf{S}}|\mathbf{M}(s,\mathbf{S}_{0})|=\sum_{\mathbf{S}_{0}\subseteq\mathbf{S}}M_{z}(s,\mathbf{S}_{0}). $$

According to Lemma 15, $M_{z}(s,\mathbf{S}_{0})\leq e^{|\mathbf{S}_{0}|-1}(ze)^{s-|\mathbf{S}_{0}|}$ . Then, we have

$$ M^{\prime}_{z}(s,\mathbf{S})\leq\sum_{\mathbf{S}_{0}\subseteq\mathbf{S}}e^{|\mathbf{S}_{0}|-1}(ze)^{s-|\mathbf{S}_{0}|}=\frac{(ze)^{s}}{e}\sum_{t=1}^{|\mathbf{S}|}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|\mathbf{S}|\\
t\\
\end{array}\right)z^{-t}=\frac{(ze)^{s}}{e}[\frac{(1+z)^{|\mathbf{S}|}}{z}-1]. $$

∎

#### Lemma 17 (Probability of equivalent error classes).

Let $H\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma\times n}$ be a $(r,c)$ -LDPC matrix, if the error $e\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ is subject to a locally stochastic noise with a noise rate $p$ , then the probability of the equivalent classes $[e]_{H}$ satisfies:

$$ \mathrm{Pr}([e]_{H}):=\sum_{e^{\prime}\in[e]_{H}}\mathrm{Pr}(e^{\prime})\leq\mathcal{O}((p/p_{z})^{|e|_{H}^{r}}) $$

if $p<p_{z}$ , where $p_{z}$ is a constant depending on $z:=(r-1)c$ .

#### Proof.

$$ \mathrm{Pr}([e]_{H})=\sum_{e^{\prime}\in[e]_{H}}\mathrm{Pr}(e)=\sum_{e_{c}\in\mathrm{ker}(H)}\mathrm{Pr}(e_{m}+e_{c}), $$

where $e_{m}$ is a minimum-weight representation in $[e]_{H}$ .

Following Ref. [1], we define a syndrome adjacency graph $G$ where we associate each of the $n$ bits with a vertex and two bits $i$ and $j$ are connected by an edge if there is a check in $H$ that acts nontrivially on both $i$ and $j$ . $G$ has a bounded vertex degree $z=(r-1)c$ . Then, any element $e_{c}\in\mathrm{ker}(H)$ has the following structure on $G$ : $e_{c}$ is always a union of connected clusters, i.e. $e_{c}=\sum_{i}e_{c}^{(i)}$ with $\{e_{c}^{(i)}\}$ being disjoint connected clusters on $G$ , where each connected cluster $e_{c}^{(i)}$ is itself in the kernel of $H$ .

Now, let $\mathbf{J}_{e_{m}}$ be the union of $\{0\}$ and the set of $e_{c}$ such that it only consists of a union of connected clusters each intersecting nontrivially with $e_{m}$ . Then we have

$$ \mathrm{Pr}([e]_{H})\leq\sum_{e_{c}\in\mathbf{J}_{e_{m}}}(\sum_{e^{\prime}\supseteq e_{m}+e_{c}}\mathrm{Pr}(e^{\prime}))=\sum_{e_{c}\in\mathbf{J}_{e_{m}}}\tilde{\mathrm{Pr}}(e_{m}+e_{c}), $$

as for any $e_{c}^{\prime}\notin\mathbf{J}_{e_{m}}$ , there exists a $e_{c}\in\mathbf{J}_{e_{m}}$ such that $e_{c}^{\prime}+e_{m}\supset e_{c}+e_{m}$ , and thus the set that is summed over in Eq. (28) is strictly larger than that in Eq. (27). Since the noise is locally stochastic, we have $\tilde{\mathrm{Pr}}(e_{m}+e_{c})\leq p^{|e_{m}+e_{c}|}$ . Furthermore, since $e_{m}$ is a minimum-weight representation, $|e_{m}+e_{c}|\geq\max\{|e_{m}|,|e_{c}|-|e_{m}|\}$ . Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}([e]_{H}) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{e_{c}\in\mathbf{J}_{e_{m}},|e_{c}|<2|e_{m}|}p^{|e_{m}|}+\sum_{e_{c}\in\mathbf{J}_{e_{m}},|e_{c}|\geq 2|e_{m}|}p^{|e_{c}|-|e_{m}|} \displaystyle=(\sum_{w=0}^{2|e_{m}|-1}n_{w})p^{|e_{m}|}+(\sum_{w=2|e_{m}|}^{\infty}n_{w}p^{w})/p^{|e_{m}|}, $$

where $n_{w}$ denotes the number of $e_{c}\in\mathbf{J}_{e_{m}}$ with weight $w$ . According to Corollary 16, we have $n_{w}=M^{\prime}_{z}(w,e_{m})\leq\frac{(ze)^{w}}{e}[(1+\frac{1}{z})^{|e_{m}|}-1]$ . Therefore,

$$ \mathrm{Pr}([e]_{H})\leq\mathcal{O}((p/p_{z})^{|e_{m}|}), $$

where $p_{z}=\frac{1}{(1+z)ze^{2}}$ , for $p<1/(ze)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 18 (Locally stochastic residual error under minimum-weight decoder).

Let $e\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ be some locally stochastic error with an error rate $p$ and a decoder returns a minimum-weight correction $e^{\prime}$ with respect to some check matrix $H\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r\times n}$ , i.e. $H(e+e^{\prime})=0$ and $e^{\prime}$ is of minimum weight among all valid corrections, then the residual error $f=e+e^{\prime}$ is locally stochastic with an error rate $\leq 2\sqrt{p}$ .

#### Proof.

Given a residual error $f$ , it is easy to see that $e$ must have a lafger intersection with $f$ : $|e\cap f|>|f|/2$ since otherwise $e^{\prime}$ would not be a minimum-weight correction. Then, we have

$$ \mathrm{Pr}(f)\leq\sum_{f_{0}\subseteq f,|f_{0}|>|f|/2}\mathrm{Pr}(e\supseteq f_{0})\leq\sum_{f_{0}\subseteq f,|f_{0}|>|f|/2}p^{|f_{0}|}=\sum_{t=|f|/2}^{|f|}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|f|\\
t\end{array}\right)p^{t}\leq(2\sqrt{p})^{|f|}. $$

∎

#### Lemma 19 (Unique-neighbor expansion [84]).

Let $G=(A\cup B,E)$ be a $(\gamma_{A},\delta_{A})$ -left-expanding graph with $\delta_{A}<1/2$ and left and right degree $\Delta_{A}$ and $\Delta_{B}$ , respectively. Let $S\subseteq A$ be any subset of $A$ , and $\Gamma_{u}(S)$ be the set of unique neighbors of $S$ , i.e. the set of vertices $v\in B$ such that $v$ has degree $1$ in the graph $S\cup\Gamma(S)$ induced by $S$ . Then, for $|S|\leq\gamma_{A}|A|$ , we have

$$ \left|\Gamma_{u}\left(S\right)\right|\geq\left(1-2\delta_{A}\right)\Delta_{A}\left|S\right|. $$

#### Corollary 20 (majority-unique neighbor condition).

Let $G=(A\cup B,E)$ be a $(\gamma_{A},\delta_{A})$ -left-expanding graph with $\delta_{A}<1/4$ . Then, for any subset $S\subseteq A$ , where $|S|\leq\gamma_{A}|A|$ , with neighbors $\Gamma(S)$ and unique neighbors $\Gamma_{u}(S)$ forming subsets in $B$ , there is at least one element $s\in S$ with majority unique neighbors, i.e. $|\Gamma_{u}(s,S)|>\frac{1}{2}|\Gamma(s,S)|$ , where $\Gamma_{u}(s,S),\Gamma(s,S)$ are the subsets of elements in $\Gamma_{u}(S),\Gamma(S)$ respectively with an edge connected to $s$ .

#### Lemma 21 (“Soundness” of HGP code).

Let $\tilde{D}_{X}$ and $\tilde{D}_{Z}$ be the $X$ and $Z$ check matrix of a HGP code $\mathrm{HGP}(H_{1},H_{2})$ with two base matrices $H_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{1}\times n_{1}}$ and $H_{2}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{2}\times n_{2}}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{D}_{X} \displaystyle=(I_{n_{1}}\otimes H_{2},H_{1}^{T}\otimes I_{r_{2}}), \displaystyle\tilde{D}_{Z} \displaystyle=(H_{1}\otimes I_{n_{2}},I_{r_{1}}\otimes H_{2}^{T}). $$

If $H_{1}^{T}$ is $(\gamma,\delta)$ -expanding with $\delta<1/4$ , then we have the following “linear soundness” relation: for any $f=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f_{a}\\ f_{b}\end{array}\right)=\tilde{D}_{Z}^{T}h\in\mathrm{im}(\tilde{D}_{Z}^{T})$ , we have

$$ |f|\geq\min\{|h|^{r}_{I_{r_{1}}\otimes H_{2}},d(H_{1}^{T}),\gamma r_{1}\}, $$

where $d(H_{1}^{T})$ denotes the distance of the classical code with check matrix $H_{1}^{T}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathbf{B}_{i}=[n_{i}]$ and $\mathbf{C}_{i}=[n_{1}+r_{1}]\backslash[n_{1}]$ denote the indices of the bits and checks of $H_{i}$ , respectively, for $i=1,2$ . $f_{a}$ , $f_{b}$ , and $h$ are supported on the 2D grids $\mathbf{B}_{1}\times\mathbf{B}_{2}$ , $\mathbf{C}_{1}\times\mathbf{C}_{2}$ , and $\mathbf{C}_{1}\times\mathbf{B}_{2}$ , respectively. We refer to $r\times(\mathbf{B}_{2}\cup\mathbf{C}_{2})$ , where $r\in{\mathbf{B}_{1}\cup\mathbf{C}_{1}}$ as a row indexed by $r$ . Given any vector $v$ , we denote $v|_{r}$ as its restriction on row $r$ , and $|v|_{\mathrm{RW}}$ (row weight of $v$ ) as the number of nonzero rows that $v$ is supported on. Given any subset $\mathbf{R}\subseteq\mathbf{C}_{1}$ and a row $r\in\mathbf{C}_{1}$ , denote $\Gamma(\mathbf{R})\subseteq\mathbf{B}_{1}$ as the neighbors of $\mathbf{R}$ and $\Gamma_{u}(r,\mathbf{R})\subseteq\Gamma(\mathbf{R})$ the unique neighbor of $r$ (see Corollary. 20) according to the Tanner graph defined by $H_{1}^{T}$ .

Observe that Eq. (34) is equivalent to proving that if $|f|\leq\min\{d(H_{1}^{T}),\gamma r_{1}\}$ , we have $|f|\geq|h|^{r}_{I_{r_{1}}\otimes H_{2}}$ . So now we assume that $|f|\leq\min\{d(H_{1}^{T}),\gamma r_{1}\}$ .

Let $\mathbf{R}\subseteq\mathbf{C}_{1}$ with $|\mathbf{R}|=q$ be the set of rows that $f_{b}$ has nontrivial supported on. By assumption, we have that $q\leq|f_{b}|\leq|f|\leq\gamma r_{1}$ . We now use an iterative proof procedure similar to that for small-set-flip decoders [85] by defining a sequence of vectors $\{f_{b}^{(i)},f_{a}^{(i)},h^{(i)}\}_{i=q,q-1,\cdots,0}$ satisfying the following conditions:

- 1. $f_{b}^{(q)}=f_{b},f_{a}^{(q)}=f_{a}|_{\Gamma(\mathbf{R})},h^{(q)}=0$ .

- 2. During step $i$ , $|f_{b}^{(i)}|_{\mathrm{RW}}=i$ .

- 3. For all $i$ , we have

$$ (I_{n_{1}}\otimes H_{2})f_{a}^{(i)}+(H_{1}^{T}\otimes H_{2})h^{(i)}=(H_{1}^{T}\otimes I_{r_{2}})f_{b}. $$

(35)

- 4. The total weight of $f_{a}$ and $h$ is non-increasing from step-to-step, i.e.

$$ |f_{a}^{(i-1)}|+|h^{(i-1)}|\leq|f_{a}^{(i)}|+|h^{(i)}|. $$

(36)

First, we check that Eq. 35 is satisfied for the initial step $i=q$ . By definitions of $f_{a}^{(q)}$ and $h^{q}$ , we are checking $(I_{n_{1}}\otimes H_{2})f_{a}|_{\Gamma(\mathbf{R})}=(H_{1}^{T}\otimes I_{r_{2}})f_{b}$ , which holds since $\tilde{D}_{X}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f_{a}\\ f_{b}\end{array}\right)=(I_{n_{1}}\otimes H_{2})f_{a}+(H_{1}^{T}\otimes I_{r_{2}})f_{b}=0$ , and $f_{a}|_{\mathbf{B}_{1}\backslash\Gamma(\mathbf{R})}=0$ by the definition of $\mathbf{R}$ . We then construct the sequence iteratively by specifying $\{f_{a}^{(i-1)},f_{b}^{(i-1)},h^{(i-1)}\}$ based on $\{f_{a}^{(i)},f_{b}^{(i)},h^{(i)}\}$ at step $i$ .

During step $i$ , assume that Eq. (35) is satisfied for $\{f_{a}^{(i)},f_{b}^{(i)},h^{(i)}\}$ and $|f_{b}^{(i)}|_{\mathrm{RW}}=i$ . Let $\mathbf{R}^{(i)}$ be the row support of $f_{b}^{(i)}$ . As $|\mathbf{R}^{(i)}|\leq q\leq\gamma|\bm{C}_{1}|$ , according to Corollary 20, we can find a row $r^{(i)}\in\mathbf{R}^{(i)}$ which has more unique neighbors in $\Gamma(\mathbf{R}^{(i)})$ than non-unique neighbors, i.e. $|\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R^{(i)}})|>|\Gamma(r^{(i)})\backslash\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R^{(i)}})|$ . We further know that $h^{(i)}|_{r^{(i)}}=0$ since otherwise we would have set $f_{b}^{(i)}|_{r^{(i)}}=0$ at the previous step $i-1$ (this will become clear after going through the assignment at step $i$ ). Then, according to Eq. (35) — $(I_{n_{1}}\otimes H_{2})f_{a}^{(i)}=(H_{1}^{T}\otimes I_{r_{2}})((I_{r_{1}}\otimes H_{2})h^{(i)}+f_{b})$ — we have that for each row $t\in\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R}^{(i)})$ ,

$$ f_{b}|_{r^{(i)}}=H_{2}f_{a}^{(i)}|_{t}. $$

In other words, we are guaranteed that $f_{b}|_{r^{(i)}}$ is a syndrome of $H_{2}$ that is generated by $\{f_{a}^{(i)}|_{t}\}_{t\in\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R}^{(i)})}$ . Let us select the minimum weight pattern, $g^{(i)}=f_{a}^{(i)}|_{t_{min}}$ , where $t_{min}=\mathrm{argmin}_{t\in\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R}^{(i)})}|f_{a}^{(i)}|_{t}|$ .

Then, we can update $h^{(i-1)}$ such that $h^{(i-1)}|_{r^{(i)}}=g^{(i)}$ and $h^{(i-1)}|_{r^{\prime}}=h^{(i)}|_{r^{\prime}}$ for all $r^{\prime}\neq r^{(i)}$ , Meanwhile, we update $f_{a}^{(i-1)}$ in the following: we set its support on all of the unique neighbors of $r^{(i)}$ to zero, i.e. $f_{a}^{(i-1)}|_{t}=0$ for all $t\in\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R}^{(i)})$ ; we add $g^{(i)}$ to $f_{a}^{(i-1)}$ on the remaining neighbors of $r^{(i)}$ , i.e. $f_{a}^{(i-1)}|_{t^{\prime}}=f_{a}^{(i)}|_{t^{\prime}}+g^{(i)}$ for all $t^{\prime}\in\Gamma(r^{(i)})\backslash\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R}^{(i)})$ ; finally, we keep $f_{a}^{(i-1)}$ the same for the remaining rows, i.e. $f_{a}^{(i-1)}|t^{\prime}=f_{a}^{(i)}|_{t^{\prime}}$ for all $t^{\prime}\in\Gamma(\mathbf{R})\backslash\Gamma(r^{(i)})$ . It is easy to verify that this guarantees Eq. (35) for step index $i-1$ . In addition, this update rule guarantees the total weight of $f_{a}^{(i)}$ and $h^{(i)}$ is non-increasing from step $i$ to step $i-1$ (Eq. (36)). In particular, notice that

$$ \displaystyle|h^{(i-1)}| \displaystyle=|h^{(i)}|+|g^{(i)}|, \displaystyle|f_{a}^{(i-1)}| \displaystyle\leq|f_{a}^{(i)}|-|g^{(i)}|, $$

where the second inequality leverages the choice of $r^{(i)}$ such that $|\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R}^{(i)})|\geq|\Gamma(r^{(i)})\backslash\Gamma_{u}(r,\mathbf{R}^{(i)})|+1$ .

Finally, we update $f_{b}^{(i-1)}$ in the following: we set $f_{b}^{(i-1)}|_{r^{(i)}}=0$ and $f_{b}^{(i-1)}|_{r^{\prime}}=f_{b}^{(i)}|_{r^{\prime}}$ for all $r^{\prime}\neq r^{(i)}$ . This guarantees that $|f_{b}^{(i-1)}|=i-1$ and also that the unique neighbors of $r^{(i)}$ , i.e. $\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R}^{(i)})$ , will not be in $\Gamma(\mathbf{R}^{(i-1)})$ .

We now prove that at the last step, when we go from $i=1$ to $i=0$ , we have $f_{a}^{(0)}=0$ . According to the update rule for $f_{a}$ , we have set $f_{a}^{(0)}|_{t}=0$ if the row $t$ is ever a unique neighbor of $r^{(i)}$ , i.e. $t\in\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R}^{(i)})$ for some $r$ . Let $\mathbf{S}:=\bigcup_{i=1}^{q}\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R}^{(i)})$ , we then have $f_{a}^{(0)}|_{\mathbf{S}}=0$ . As such, we simply need to prove that $\mathbf{S}=\Gamma(\mathbf{R})$ . Note that for any $r\in\Gamma(r^{(i)})\backslash\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i)},\mathbf{R}^{(i)})$ that is a non-unique neighbor of $r^{(i)}$ , it will become the unique neighbor of some $r^{(i^{\prime})}$ with $i^{\prime}<i$ , i.e. $r\in\Gamma_{u}(r^{(i^{\prime})},\mathbf{R}^{(i^{\prime})})$ . Therefore, we have $\mathbf{S}\supseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{q}\Gamma(r^{(i)})=\Gamma(\mathbf{R})$ .

Then, $h^{(0)}$ satisfies $(H_{1}^{T}\otimes I_{r_{2}})[f_{b}+(I_{r_{1}}\otimes H_{2})h^{(0)}]=0$ (according to Eq. (35) at $i=0$ ) and $|h^{(0)}|\leq|f_{a}|$ (according to Eq. (36)). Since $|f_{b}+(I_{r_{1}}\otimes H_{2})h^{(0)}|_{\mathrm{RW}}\leq|f_{b}|+|h^{(0)}|\leq|f|$ , which is less than $d(H_{1}^{T})$ (by assumption), we have $(I_{r_{1}}\otimes H_{2})h^{(0)}=f_{b}$ . This indicates that $h^{(0)}\in[h]_{I_{r_{1}}\otimes H_{2}}$ . Therefore, we have $[h]^{r}_{I_{r_{1}}\otimes H_{2}}\leq|h^{(0)}|\leq|f_{a}|\leq|f|$ .

∎

Note that Eq. (34) is not the same the standard soundness definition for HGP codes [36]. As we will show later, the detector-fault matrices Eqs. (20)(21) of the BSE gadget coincide with the check matrices of some HGP code, and we will use Eq. (34) to upper-bound the size of the effective residual error (corresponding to $h$ ) by that of the circuit fault (corresponding to $f$ ), which is the key ingredient behind the fault tolerance of the BSE gadget.

#### S1.3.2 Proof for the residual $X$ syndrome error $r^{Z}_{s}$

The $X$ detectors for correcting a $Z$ -type error $e^{Z}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}e^{Z}_{d}\\ e^{Z}_{s}\end{array}\right)$ are given by Eq. (20). $D_{X}$ corresponds to the $X$ check matrix of a HGP code $\mathcal{C}^{Z}=\mathrm{HGP}(H_{C}^{T},H_{q,X})$ , whose $Z$ check matrix is

$$ \tilde{D}_{Z}=\left(H_{C}^{T}\otimes I_{n},I_{n_{C}}\otimes H_{X}^{T}\right). $$

By assumption, $H_{C}$ is full rank. Then, accoring to Ref. [41], $\mathcal{C}^{Z}$ has dimension $k(H_{C}^{T})k(H_{X})+k(H_{C})k(H_{X}^{T})=k(H_{C})k(H_{X}^{T})$ , where $k(H_{i})$ denotes the dimension of the kernel of $H_{i}$ . A logical $Z$ operator basis is given by $\left(0,\mathrm{ker}(H_{C})\otimes\mathrm{im}^{\bullet}(H_{X})\right)$ [42, 16]. One can show that such a basis cannot be weight-reduced below $d_{C}$ , and thus the $Z$ distance of $\mathcal{C}^{Z}$ is $d_{C}$ .

After a minimum-weight correction $e^{Z\prime}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}e^{Z\prime}_{d}\\ e^{Z\prime}_{s}\end{array}\right)$ , the residual fault $f^{Z}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f^{Z}_{d}\\ f^{Z}_{s}\\ \end{array}\right):=e^{Z}+e^{Z\prime}$ will be in the kernel of $D_{X}$ (i.e. $D_{X}f^{Z}=0$ ), which could be either a $Z$ logical operator or a $Z$ check of $\mathcal{C}^{Z}$ . If $|f^{Z}|<d_{C}$ , then $f^{Z}$ has to be a $Z$ check, i.e. $f^{Z}=\tilde{D}_{Z}^{T}h^{Z}$ for some $h^{Z}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n_{C}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ . In addition, according to Lemma 18, $f^{Z}$ is locally stochastic with an error rate $2\sqrt{p}$ .

Based on the assumption, $H_{C}$ is $(\gamma,\delta)$ -expanding with $\delta<1/4$ . Then, according to Lemma. 21, we have

$$ |f^{Z}|\geq\min\{|h^{Z}|^{r}_{I_{n_{C}}\otimes H_{X}},d_{C},\gamma n_{C}\}=\min\{|h^{Z}|^{r}_{I_{n_{C}}\otimes H_{X}},\Theta(d)\}, $$

where we implicitly use that $d_{C}=\Theta(d)$ and $\gamma n_{C}=\Theta(d)$ for a good $[n_{C}=\Theta(d_{C}),k_{C}=\Theta(d_{C}),d_{C}=\Theta(d)]$ classical code $H_{C}$ .

Let $h^{Z}_{m}$ be a minimum-weight representative among $[h^{Z}]_{I_{n_{C}}\otimes H_{X}}$ . This indicates that the residual syndrome error $f^{Z}_{s}$ is the boundary of some effective data error $h^{Z}_{m}$ on the blocks $\bm{B}_{0}\cup\bm{B}_{1}$ , whose weight is upper bounded by the weight of the fault $f^{Z}$ in the circuit provided that $f^{Z}$ is not too large.

Now, we prove that the distribution of $h^{Z}_{m}$ is locally stochastic. Let $f^{Z}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f^{Z}_{d}\\ f^{Z}_{s}\end{array}\right)$ be one fault configuration that gives rise to a target $h^{Z}_{m}$ . Clearly, any other fault $f^{Z\prime}$ that also gives rise to the same $h^{Z}_{m}$ belong to the class $\left(\begin{array}[]{c}[f^{Z}_{d}]_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{X}}\\ f^{Z}_{s}\end{array}\right)$ , which we simply denote as $[f^{Z}]_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{X}}$ , and it satisfies $|f^{Z\prime}|\geq\min\{|h^{Z}_{m}|,\Theta(d)\}$ . This indicates that

$$ |f^{Z}|^{r}_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{X}}\geq\min\{|h^{Z}_{m}|,\Theta(d)\}. $$

Therefore, we have

$$ \mathrm{Pr}(f^{Z}_{s}=(I_{n_{C}}\otimes H_{X})h^{Z}_{m})\leq\mathrm{Pr}([f^{Z}]_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{X}})\leq\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{p})^{|f^{Z}_{d}|_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{X}}^{r}}\leq\mathcal{O}(p)^{\min\{|h^{Z}_{m}|,\Theta(d)\}/2}, $$

where the second equality utilizes Lemma. 17, and the third equality utilizes Eq. (41). This proves the property of the residual syndrome error in Eq. (22) in the limit $d\rightarrow\infty$ .

#### S1.3.3 Proof for the residual $X$ data error $r^{X}$

The $Z$ detectors for correcting an error $e^{X}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}e^{X}_{d}\\ e^{X}_{s}\end{array}\right)$ are given by Eq. (21). $D_{Z}$ corresponds to the $X$ check matrix of a HGP code $\mathcal{C}^{X}=\mathrm{HGP}(H_{C}^{1},H_{Z})$ , whose associated $Z$ check matrix is

$$ \tilde{D}_{X}=\left(H_{C}^{1}\otimes I_{n},I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z}^{T}\right). $$

By assumption, $H_{C}^{1}$ is full rank, and thus $\mathcal{C}^{X}$ encodes no logical qubits and has a distance $\infty$ .

After a perfect minimum-weight correction $e^{X\prime}=(e^{X\prime}_{d},e^{X\prime}_{s})$ , the residual fault $f^{X}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f^{X}_{d}\\ f^{X}_{s}\\ \end{array}\right):=e^{X}+e^{X\prime}$ will be in the kernel of $D_{Z}$ (i.e. $D_{Z}f^{X}=0$ ) and satisfies $f^{X}=\tilde{D}_{X}^{T}h^{X}$ for some $h^{X}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\sigma_{C}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ . In addition, according to Lemma 18, $f^{X}$ is locally stochastic with an error rate $2\sqrt{p}$ .

By assumption, $(H_{C}^{1})^{T}$ is $(\gamma,\delta)$ -left expanding with $\delta<1/4$ . According to Lemma. 21, we have

$$ |f^{X}|\geq\min\{|h^{X}|^{r}_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z}},d((H_{C}^{1})^{T}))=\infty,\gamma r_{C}\}=\min\{|h^{X}|^{r}_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z}},\Theta(d)\}. $$

Let $h^{X}_{m}$ be the minimum-weight representative among the equivalent class $[h^{X}]_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z}}$ , we then have $|f^{X}|\geq\min\{|h^{X}_{m}|,\Theta(d)\}$ . Here, we further introduce $h^{X\prime}_{m}:=\min_{s^{\prime}\in\mathrm{im}(I_{\sigma_{C}\otimes H_{X}})}h^{X}+s^{\prime}$ , which is the minimum weight representative of the coset of $h^{X}$ with respect to the $X$ checks. Note that $h^{X}_{m}$ and $h^{X\prime}_{m}$ could differ by a logical $X$ operator. Nevertheless, we now prove that $h^{X}_{m}=h^{X\prime}_{m}$ if $|f^{X}|<d/(2\Delta)$ , where $\Delta$ denotes the maximum row- and column-weight of $H_{C}$ . We prove this by contradiction. Assume that $h^{X}=h^{X}_{m}+h^{\prime}$ , where $h^{\prime}\in\mathrm{ker}(I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z})$ contains some nontrivial logical $X$ operators $\mathcal{Q}$ distributed on set of blocks in $\bm{A}$ , we have

$$ |f^{X}_{d}|=|((H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{n})(h^{X}_{m}+h^{\prime})|\geq|((H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{\prime}|-|((H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{X}_{m}|\geq|((H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{\prime}|-\Delta|h^{X}_{m}|>|((H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{\prime}|-d/2, $$

where the second last inequality uses that $|((H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{X}_{m}|\leq\Delta|h^{X}_{m}|$ since the row- and column-weight of $(H_{C}^{1})^{T}$ is bounded by $\Delta$ and the last equality uses $|h^{X}_{m}|\leq|f^{X}|<d/(2\Delta)$ . Now, since $\mathrm{ker}((H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{n})=0$ as $H_{C}^{1}$ is full rank, $((H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{\prime}$ contains at least one nontrivial logical $X$ operators of $\mathcal{Q}$ distributed in some block of $\bm{A}$ . Therefore, we end up with $|f^{X}_{d}|>|((H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{\prime}|-d/2>d-d/2=d/2$ , which contradicts the assumption that $|f^{X}_{d}|\leq|f^{X}|<d/(2\Delta)$ for $\Delta\geq 1$ . Thus, we conclude that $h^{X}=h^{X}_{m}+s$ for some $s\in\mathrm{im}(I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{X})$ , which indicates that $h^{X\prime}_{m}=h^{X}_{m}$ . Consequently, we have $|f^{X}|\geq\min\{|h^{X\prime}_{m}|,\Theta(d)\}$

Now, we prove that $h^{X\prime}_{m}$ is subject to a locally stochastic distribution. Let $f^{X}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f^{X}_{d}\\ f^{X}_{s}\end{array}\right)$ be one fault configuration that gives rise to a target $h^{X\prime}_{m}$ . Clearly, any other fault $f^{X\prime}$ that also gives rise to the same $h^{X\prime}_{m}$ belong to the class $\left(\begin{array}[]{c}[f^{X}_{d}]_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z}}\\ f^{X}_{s}\end{array}\right)$ , which we simply denote as $[f^{X}]_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z}}$ , and it satisfies $|f^{\prime X}|\geq\min\{|h^{X\prime}_{m}|,\Theta(d)\}$ . This indicates that

$$ |f^{X}|^{r}_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z}}\geq\min\{|h^{X\prime}_{m}|,\Theta(d)\}. $$

As such, we have

$$ \mathrm{Pr}(h^{X\prime}_{m})\leq\mathrm{Pr}([f^{X}]_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z}})\leq\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{p})^{|f^{X}|_{I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{Z}}^{r}}\leq\mathcal{O}(p)^{\min\{|h^{\prime X}_{m}|,\Theta(d)\}/2}, $$

where the second equality utilizes Lemma. 17 and the third equality utilizes Eq. (46). This indicates that $h^{X\prime}_{m}$ is locally stochastic in the limit $d\rightarrow\infty$ .

Finally, we prove that the residual output error $r^{X}$ on $\bm{B}_{0}$ can be written as the propagation of $h^{X\prime}_{m}$ through a constant depth circuit, thereby also being locally stochastic.

The output residual error $r^{X}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k_{C}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ on the block $\mathbf{B}_{0}$ is given by

$$ r^{X}=((H_{C}^{0})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{X}=((H_{C}^{0})^{T}\otimes I_{n})(h^{X\prime}_{m}+s^{\prime}). $$

for some $s^{\prime}\in\mathrm{im}(I_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{X})$ . Here, the first equality can be seen from the following: the residual error $r^{X}$ is propagated from the residual fault $f^{X}_{d}$ and $f^{X}_{s}$ . The syndrome fault $f^{X}_{s}$ is equivalent to two layers of data errors $h^{X}$ before and after the $X$ syndrome extraction on $\bm{A}$ . The error $h^{X}$ before the syndrome extraction can be absorbed to the initial $X$ -basis preparation of $\bm{A}$ and thus will not contribute to $r^{X}$ , whereas the error $h^{X}$ after the syndrome extraction will propagate though the transversal CNOTs to (1) $\bm{B}_{1}$ in the form $((H_{C}^{1})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{X}$ , which cancels $f^{X}_{d}$ (2) $\bm{B}_{0}$ in the form of $((H_{C}^{0})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{X}$ , which gives the residual error $r^{X}$ .

Since the BSE gadget measures a round of $X$ checks of the quantum code, i.e. ${I}_{k_{C}}\otimes H_{X}$ , at the beginning, the $\mathbf{B}_{0}$ block will be in the eigenstates of ${I}_{\sigma_{C}}\otimes H_{X}$ . As such, we are free to remove $s^{\prime}$ in Eq. (48) and set $r^{X}=((H_{C}^{0})^{T}\otimes I_{n})h^{X\prime}_{m}$ . This indicates that the residual error $r^{X}$ is propagated from $h^{X\prime}$ via a constant depth circuit. Finally, according to Lemma 5.2 of Ref. [17], $r^{X}$ is also locally stochastic if $h^{X\prime}$ is locally stochastic.

#### S1.3.4 Existence of $H_{C}$

Our proofs of the fault tolerance of BSE in Theorem 14 relied on the existence of an LDPC classical code $H_{C}$ with certain expansion properties. In particular, we need $H_{C}$ to be an expander code, and also need a sub-matrix of its transpose, $(H_{C}^{1})^{T}$ , to be an expander code. In this section, we discuss how to ensure these conditions are satisfied, and argue that an asymptotically good family of classical random codes can be easily constructed and made to satisfy these conditions (see Prop. 23).

#### Definition 22 (Random regular bipartite graph [84] (configuration model)).

To construct a bipartite graph with a bit degree $c$ and a check degree $r$ , we first choose a random matching between $N=crm$ “left” nodes and $N$ “right” nodes. We then collapse consecutive sets of $c$ left nodes to form the $rm$ degree- $c$ bits and collapse consecutive sets of $r$ right nodes to form the $cm$ degree- $r$ checks. This gives the random bipartite graph $G(\mathbf{V_{C}}\cup\mathbf{V_{V}},\mathbf{E})$ . The bipartite adjacency matrix of $G$ gives the check matrix $H_{C}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{(cm)\times(rm)}$ of the constructed classical code. We denote such a random ensemble as $\bm{\mathrm{LDPC}}(m,r,c)$ .

We construct the target $H_{C}=(H_{C}^{0},H_{C}^{1})$ by taking $H_{C}^{0}$ and $H_{C}^{1}$ independently from the ensemble in Def. 22:

$$ H_{C}^{0}\in\bm{\mathrm{LDPC}}(m,\Delta_{c}^{0},\Delta_{v});\quad H_{C}^{1}\in\bm{\mathrm{LDPC}}(m,\Delta_{v},\Delta_{v}). $$

Then, $H_{C}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\Delta_{v}\times m(\Delta_{c}^{0}+\Delta_{v})}$ with a check degree $\Delta_{c}^{0}+\Delta_{v}$ and a bit degree $\Delta_{v}$ . Denoting $r_{c}=m\Delta_{v}$ , $n_{c}^{0}=m\Delta_{c}^{0}$ and $n_{c}^{1}=m\Delta_{v}$ , we have $H_{C}^{0}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{c}\times n_{c}^{0}}$ and $H_{C}^{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{c}\times n_{c}^{1}}$ .

#### Proposition 23 (Existence of classical code $H_{c}$ for Theorem 14).

A random classical code $H_{c}$ constructed using Eq. (49) satisfies the requirements in Theorem 14 — $H_{C}$ and $(H_{C}^{1})^{T}$ are $(\gamma,\delta)$ -left expanding for some constant $\gamma$ and $\delta<1/4$ and $H_{C}^{1}$ is full rank — with high probability when $\Delta_{v}\gg 1$ .

#### Proof.

We first prove that $H_{C}^{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{c}\times n_{c}^{1}}$ , with $r_{c}=n_{c}^{1}$ , is full rank with high probability. According to Ref. [86],

$$ \mathrm{lim}_{n_{c}^{1}\rightarrow\infty}\mathrm{Rank}(H_{C}^{1})/n_{c}^{1}=1-\max_{\beta\in[0,1]}\Phi(\beta), $$

with high probability, where

$$ \Phi(\beta):=D_{c}\left(1-D_{v}^{\prime}(\beta)/\Delta_{v}\right)-\left(1-D_{v}(\beta)-(1-\beta)D_{v}^{\prime}(\beta)\right), $$

where $D_{c}(x)$ and $D_{v}(x)$ are polynomials in $x$ with coefficients being the check- and bit-degree distribution of $H_{C}^{1}$ , respectively. In our case, we have $D_{c}(x)=D_{v}(x)=x^{\Delta_{v}}$ , and $\max_{\beta\in[0,1]}\Phi(\beta)=0$ [87], which concludes that $H_{C}^{1}$ has full rank with high probability.

Next, we prove that both $(H_{C}^{1})^{T}$ and $H_{C}$ are left expanding with high probability. Consider the bipartite Tanner graph $G(\bm{C}\cup\bm{B},\bm{E})$ of $H_{C}$ , whose bit nodes $\bm{B}$ are further decomposed into $\bm{B}^{0}\cup\bm{B}^{1}$ , where $\bm{B}^{0}$ with $|\bm{B}^{0}|=n_{c}^{0}$ and $\bm{B}^{1}$ with $|\bm{B}^{1}|=n_{c}^{1}$ are associated with the columns of $H_{C}^{0}$ and $H_{C}^{1}$ , respectively. Given any $\bm{S}\subseteq\bm{B}$ (resp. $\bm{S}_{c}\subseteq\bm{C}$ ), we denote its neighbor in $\bm{C}$ (resp. $\bm{B}$ ) as $\Gamma(\bm{S})$ (resp. $\Gamma_{c}(\bm{S}_{c})$ ). In addition, give any $\bm{S}\subseteq\bm{B}$ , we denote its restriction on $\bm{B}^{1}$ as $\bm{S}|_{\bm{B}^{1}}$ . We first show the following properties for $G$ :

- 1. For any $\mathbf{S}_{c}\subset\bm{C}$ with $|\mathbf{S}_{c}|=\alpha_{c}|\bm{C}|$ , where $0<\alpha_{c}<1$ , we have

$$ |\Gamma_{c}(\mathbf{S}_{c})|_{\bm{B}^{1}}|\geq|\bm{C}|\Delta_{v}\left(\frac{1}{\Delta_{v}}\left(1-(1-\alpha_{c})^{\Delta_{v}}\right)-\sqrt{2\alpha_{c}H(\alpha_{c})/(\Delta_{v}\log_{2}e})\right), $$

(52) where $H(\bullet)$ denotes the binary entropy function.

- 2. For any $\bm{S}=\bm{S}^{0}\cup\bm{S}^{1}$ with $|\bm{S}|=\alpha|\bm{B}|$ , where $\bm{S}^{0}\subseteq\bm{B}^{0}$ with $|\bm{S}^{0}|=\alpha_{0}|\bm{B}^{0}|$ and $\bm{S}^{1}\subseteq\bm{B}^{1}$ with $|\bm{S}^{1}|=\alpha_{1}|\bm{B}^{1}|$ , we have

$$ |\Gamma(\mathbf{S})|\geq|\bm{B}|\Delta_{v}\left[\frac{|\bm{C}|}{|\bm{B}|\Delta_{v}}\left(1-(1-\alpha_{0})^{\Delta_{c}^{0}}(1-\alpha_{1})^{\Delta_{v}}\right)-\sqrt{2\alpha H(\alpha)/(\Delta_{v}\log_{2}e})\right]. $$

(53)

The first property is related to the expansion of $(H_{C}^{1})^{T}$ and is proved in Ref. [84] as $H_{C}^{1}$ is constructed independently. Here, we extend the proof in Ref. [84] for the second property, which is related to the expansion of the joint matrix $H_{C}$ .

We first consider the probability that a given check node $c$ in $\bm{C}$ is not a neighbor of $\mathbf{S}$ . Each neighbor of $c$ in $\bm{B}^{0}$ (resp. $\bm{B}^{1}$ ) is in the set $\bm{S}^{0}$ (resp. $\bm{S}^{1}$ ) with probability $\alpha_{0}$ (resp. $\alpha_{1}$ ). Thus the probability that $c\notin\Gamma(\bm{S})$ is

$$ \left(\prod_{i=0}^{\Delta_{c}^{0}-1}\frac{n_{c}^{0}-\alpha_{0}n_{c}^{0}-i}{n_{c}^{0}-i}\right)\left(\prod_{i=0}^{\Delta_{v}-1}\frac{n_{c}^{1}-\alpha_{1}n_{c}^{1}-i}{n_{c}^{1}-i}\right)\approx(1-\alpha_{0})^{\Delta_{c}^{0}}(1-\alpha_{1})^{\Delta_{v}}, $$

as $n_{c}^{0},n_{c}^{1}\rightarrow\infty$ . This implies that the expected value of $|\bm{C}\backslash\Gamma(\bm{S})|$ is $|\bm{C}|(1-\alpha_{0})^{\Delta_{c}^{0}}(1-\alpha_{1})^{\Delta_{v}}$ , and consequently, the expected value of $|\Gamma(\bm{S})|_{\bm{B}^{1}}|$ is

$$ |\bm{C}|\left(1-(1-\alpha_{0})^{\Delta_{c}^{0}}(1-\alpha_{1})^{\Delta_{v}}\right). $$

In the following, we prove that with high probability, $|\Gamma(\bm{S})|_{\mathbf{V_{1}}}|$ only deviates from this expected value by a small amount using a martingale argument [84].

Each node in $\bm{S}$ will have $\Delta_{v}$ outgoing edges, so there are in total $N:=\Delta_{v}|\bm{S}|$ outgoing edges from $\bm{S}$ . We consider the random process in which the destinations of these edges are revealed one at a time. We let $X_{i}$ be the random variable equal to the expected size of the set of neighbors of $\bm{S}$ given that the first $i$ edges leaving $\bm{S}$ have been revealed. Namely, let $x_{i}\in\{0,1\}$ be the random variable indicating if revealing the $i$ -th edge adds a new neighbor in $\bm{C}$ to the known neighbors of $\bm{S}$ in $\bm{C}$ , then we have $X_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{i}x_{j}+E[\sum_{j=i+1}^{N}x_{j}]$ . In particular, we have $X_{0}=E[\sum_{j=1}^{N}x_{j}]$ , which is the expected value of $|\Gamma(\bm{S})|$ , and $X_{N}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}x_{j}$ , which is the actual value of $|\Gamma(\bm{S})|$ . $\{X_{i}\}_{i=0}^{N}$ forms a martingale since

$$ E[X_{i}|\{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{i-1}]=E[\sum_{j=1}^{i}x_{j}+E[\sum_{j=i+1}^{N}x_{j}]|\{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{i-1}]=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}x_{j}+E[\sum_{j=i}^{N}x_{j}]=X_{i-1}. $$

Moreover, $|X_{i+1}-X_{i}|\leq 1$ for all $0\leq i<N$ . Thus by Azuma’s Inequality [88], we have

$$ \mathrm{Pr}(|X_{N}-X_{0}|>\lambda\sqrt{N})<e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}, $$

Since there are only $\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|\bm{B}|\\ \alpha|\bm{B}|\end{array}\right)$ choices for $\mathbf{S}$ , it suffices to choose $\lambda$ so that

$$ \binom{|\bm{B}|}{\alpha|\bm{B}|}e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}\ll 1. $$

Using Stirling’s formula, this holds for large $n_{c}$ if $\lambda$ satisfies

$$ \frac{|\bm{B}|H(\alpha)}{\log_{2}^{e}}<\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\Rightarrow\lambda>\sqrt{2|\bm{B}|H(\alpha)/\log_{2}^{e}}, $$

which gives the second property (Eq. (53)).

Now, we prove that $(H_{C}^{1})^{T}$ and $H_{C}$ can be both $(\gamma,\delta)$ -left expanding using Eq. (52) and Eq. (53), respectively. Following Ref. [84], we assume that $\alpha_{c}=|\bm{S}_{c}|/|\bm{C}|$ and $\alpha=|\bm{S}|/|\bm{B}|$ are constants. In addition, we assume $\Delta_{c}^{0}<\Delta_{v}$ , which corresponds to the case where the rate of $H_{C}$ is less than $1/2$ . When $\alpha_{c}\Delta_{v}$ and $\alpha\Delta$ is much smaller than $1$ , Eq. (52) and Eq. (53) are approximated by

$$ \displaystyle|\Gamma_{c}(\bm{S}_{c})|_{\bm{B}^{1}}|/(\Delta_{v}|\bm{S}_{c}|) \displaystyle\geq 1-\sqrt{\frac{2H(\alpha_{c})}{\log_{2}^{e}\alpha_{c}\Delta_{v}}}, \displaystyle|\Gamma(\bm{S})|/(\Delta_{v}|\bm{S}|) \displaystyle\geq 1-\sqrt{\frac{2H(\alpha)}{\log_{2}^{e}\alpha\Delta_{v}}}, $$

where we have used that $(1-\alpha_{c})^{\Delta_{v}}\approx 1-\Delta_{v}\alpha_{c}$ , $(1-\alpha_{0})^{\Delta_{c}^{0}}\approx 1-\Delta_{c}^{0}\alpha_{0}$ , and $(1-\alpha_{1})^{\Delta_{v}}\approx 1-\Delta_{v}\alpha_{1}$ . This indicates that both $H_{C}$ and $(H_{C}^{1})^{T}$ are $(\gamma,\delta)$ -expanding when $\Delta_{v}=\Omega(1/\delta^{2})$ and $\gamma=\mathcal{O}(1/\Delta_{v})$ . We note that such proof of expansion from Ref. [84], which utilizes the lower bounds in Eq. (60), implicitly relies on that we only consider constant fractions of graph nodes as $H(\alpha)/\alpha$ diverges as $\alpha\rightarrow 0$ . For smaller subsets, e.g. $\alpha_{c}=\mathcal{O}(1/r_{c})$ and $\alpha=\mathcal{O}(1/n_{c})$ , the lower bound here is likely loose and one would need to use tighter element-counting lower bounds(e.g. the proof for Theorem 8.7 in [34]) for the neighbors.

Since $H_{C}^{1}$ is full-rank with high probability, this family has a constant rate $\Delta_{c}^{0}/(\Delta_{c}^{0}+\Delta_{v})$ . In addition, the expansion of $H_{C}$ implies that these codes have a distance that scale linearly with the block length [84]. As such, we can increase the distance of $H_{c}$ until it matches with the quantum-code distance by increasing the block length. ∎

### S1.4 Connection to cluster-state schemes

As illustrated in Fig. 12, the BSE gadget for measuring $Z$ checks can be viewed as the generalization of the foliated cluster-state protocol in Ref. [32] by replacing the underlying repetition code with a high-rate classical code. See the caption of Fig. 12 for details. Note that the repetition-code construction in Ref. 12 indicates that the classical code being expanding is only a sufficient condition for guaranteeing the fault tolerance of the BSE gadget, and one might be table to find weaker conditions.

*Figure 12: Connection between the BSE gadget and the cluster-state protocol in Ref. [32]. A BSE gadget for preparing the logical $\overline{\ket{+}}$ states of the blocks $\bm{B}_{0}$ using a repetition code (a) is equivalent to the circuit in (b), where the $\bm{A}$ blocks are initialized and measured in the $X$ basis and the $X$ checks on the $\bm{A}$ are measured in the $Z$ basis, i.e. measuring $H^{\otimes n}S_{X}H^{\otimes n}$ . The circuit in (b) exactly prepares the foliated-code cluster state (c) before the final transversal $X$ measurements. By then performing the transversal $X$ measurements on blocks $\bm{B}_{1}$ and $\bm{A}$ in (a) and (b), which corresponds to measuring out the bulk of the 3D cluster state in (c), the protocol outputs the blocks $\bm{B}_{0}$ encoded in the logical $\overline{\ket{+}}^{\otimes k}$ of the target $[[n,k,d]]$ quantum code (with a feedback $Z$ correction based on the measurement outcomes on $\bm{B}_{1}$ ). The primal and dual layer of the foliated code in (c) corresponds to the bits and the checks of the classical repetition code, and the nearest-block connections of the foliated code correspond to the connections of the Tanner graph of the repetition code. The $X$ and $Z$ detectors of the BSE gadget in (a) and (b) correspond to the primal and dual stabilizers of the foliated code, respectively. Therefore, the cluster-state protocol in Ref. [32] corresponds to a special-case BSE gadget using a repetition code. A high-rate BSE gadget is equivalent to preparing a generalized foliated code involving a $[n_{C},k_{C},d_{C}]$ classical code $\mathcal{C}$ with $k_{C}>1$ , measuring out its “bulk” corresponding to the $n_{C}-k_{C}$ bits and the $n_{C}-k_{C}$ checks of $\mathcal{C}$ , and outputting its “boundary” corresponding to the $k_{C}$ bits of $\mathcal{C}$ .*
