### S1.5 Single-shot code surgery using BSE

*Figure 13: Illustration of single-shot lattice surgery using BSE. To perform $XX$ measurements on a batch of paired surface codes, we (1) prepare the ancilla qubits (the grey qubits on the orange strip $\mathcal{A}$ ) in $\ket{0}$ , (2) measure all the $X$ stabilizers on the merged codes using the BSE gadget, (3) meausre the ancilla qubits in the $Z$ basis (with $X$ feedback on the output codes).*

Here, we show how the BSE gadget can be used for performing batched code surgeries in single shot. We first illustrate this for performing standard lattice surgery between two surface code patches [25] and then generalize it to the recent surgery techniques for generic qLDPC codes [26, 13].

As shown in Fig. 13, we first consider two surface code patches $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ with distance $d$ and perform a standard $\bar{X}_{1}\bar{X}_{2}$ logical measurement by introducing a thin strip of ancilla system $\mathcal{A}$ at the interface of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ [25]. The $\bar{X}_{1}\bar{X}_{2}$ measurement outcome is obtained by taking the product of the interface $X$ checks $\mathcal{S}_{m}$ on $\mathcal{A}$ , which are part of the stabilizers of the merged code (see step (2) in Fig. 13). Conventionally, we need to repeat $\mathcal{O}(d)$ rounds of stabilizer measurements for the merged code to reliably infer the values of $\mathcal{S}_{m}$ so that we obtain the correct $\bar{X}_{1}\bar{X}_{2}$ measurement. Here, we show that a single round suffices if we measure the merged code stabilizers using the BSE gadget.

Here we consider a phenomenological noise model and focus on $Z$ -type errors, i.e. $Z$ data errors and syndrome errors on $X$ checks since the analysis for the other type of error is trivial. We assume that the two individual surface code patches have been fault-tolerantly prepared, i.e. the stabilizers have all been fixed to $+1$ , with some residual noise $e_{1}$ (see Fig. 13(1)) that is local stochastic with parameter $p$ . Although we assume here that all stabilizers have been fixed to $+1$ , other patterns can be easily incorporated via standard Pauli frame tracking methods. After performing the syndrome correction using the BSE gadget, we obtain some syndrome $S=S|_{\mathcal{Q}_{1}\cup\mathcal{Q}_{2}}\cup S|_{\mathcal{A}}$ , whose component $S|_{\mathcal{Q}_{1}\cup\mathcal{Q}_{2}}$ on the data codes should be deterministic while component $S|_{\mathcal{A}}$ on the ancilla system is non-deterministic, in the absence of errors. We then perform a final correction $\hat{e}$ based on $S|_{\mathcal{Q}_{1}\cup\mathcal{Q}_{2}}$ assuming only data errors using, e.g. the matching decoder. We aim to show that, after such corrections, we can obtain the true measurement outcome for $\bar{X}_{1}\bar{X}_{2}$ with high probability $1-\mathcal{O}(p^{d/4})$ .

According to Theorem 14, the syndromes of the merged code are measured fault-tolerantly, up to residual syndrome errors that form the boundary of some locally stochastic $Z$ data errors. Therefore, we can write the measured syndrome as $S=S_{0}\oplus\partial(e_{1})\oplus\partial(e_{2})$ , where $S_{0}$ are the true syndrome values in the absence of errors, which satisfies $S_{0}|_{\mathcal{Q}_{1},\mathcal{Q}_{2}}=0$ , and $e_{2}$ is the equivalent local stochastic data noise of the BSE syndrome measurements (see Fig. 13(2)). Here, $\partial$ denotes the boundary map of the merged code associate with the $X$ checks. Based on $S$ , we infer a data-error correction $\hat{e}$ supported on $\mathcal{Q}_{1}\cup\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ satisfying $(\partial(\hat{e})+S)|_{\mathcal{Q}_{1}\cup\mathcal{Q}_{2}}=0$ . Therefore, we have that $\partial(\hat{e}\oplus e_{1}\oplus e_{2})|_{\mathcal{Q}_{1},\mathcal{Q}_{2}}=0$ . Since $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ are local stochastic with parameter $p$ , $e_{1}\oplus e_{2}$ is local stochastic with parameter $\sqrt{p}$ . Since the recovery is given by a minimum weight decoder, $|\hat{e}|\leq|e_{1}\oplus e_{2}|$ . Therefore, with probability $1-\mathcal{O}(p^{d/4})$ , $|\hat{e}\oplus e_{1}\oplus e_{2}|<d$ . Since $\partial(\hat{e}\oplus e_{1}\oplus e_{2})|_{\mathcal{Q}_{1},\mathcal{Q}_{2}}=0$ , we conclude that with high probability, $(\hat{e}\oplus e_{1}\oplus e_{2})|_{\mathcal{Q}_{1},\mathcal{Q}_{2}}$ must act as a stabilizer on $\mathcal{Q}_{1},\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ .

The true logical measurement is obtained by taking the product of syndromes in $S_{0}|_{\mathcal{A}}$ . The actual (corrected) logical measurement result returned from our procedure is the product of $(S\oplus\partial\hat{e})|_{\mathcal{A}}=S_{0}|_{\mathcal{A}}\oplus(\partial(e_{1}\oplus e_{2}\oplus\hat{e}))|_{\mathcal{A}}$ . Therefore, our deduced logical measurement result differs from the ideal result by the product of $\partial(e_{1}\oplus e_{2}\oplus\hat{e})|_{\mathcal{A}}$ . Since $e_{1}\oplus e_{2}\oplus\hat{e}$ acts as a stabilizer on $\mathcal{Q}_{1},\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ with high probability, its action on those qubits must commute with all stabilizers of the merged code, including $\bar{X}_{1}\bar{X}_{2}$ , and thus not affect the logical measurement result. The only remaining contribution must come from its restriction to the qubits on $\mathcal{A}$ . However, since the product of the checks on $\mathcal{A}$ is simply $\bar{X}_{1}\bar{X}_{2}$ and does not support on $\mathcal{A}$ , it will also not affect the logical measurement. Therefore, with probability $1-\mathcal{O}(p^{d/4})$ , the logical measurement result will be correct.

We can also generalize the preceding analysis to more general surgery constructions. Consider the homological measurement framework for general code surgeries [90, 14, 13, 43] and a surgery protocol that involves two qlDPC codes $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\prime}$ along with an adapter system $\mathcal{A}$ in Def. 24. The preceding discussion implies that the ideal logical measurement result and inferred logical measurement result differ by certain products of the syndromes in $\partial(e_{1}\oplus e_{2}\oplus\hat{e})|_{\mathcal{A}}$ .

In the language of Def. 24, we can write the effective data error $e_{1}\oplus e_{2}\oplus\hat{e}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}a\\
b\\
c\end{pmatrix}, $$

where the three components act on the data qubits in $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ , $\mathcal{A}$ , $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\prime}$ respectively. The boudary map $\partial$ is given by the $X$ check matrix of the merged code:

$$ \tilde{H}_{X}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}H_{x}&0&0\\
f_{1}^{T}&\partial_{1}^{T}&f_{1}^{\prime T}\\
0&0&H_{x}^{\prime}\\
\end{array}\right), $$

where the three rows are associated with the $X$ syndromes on $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ , $\mathcal{A}$ , and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ , respectively.

The logical measurements $\{\bar{X}_{i}\bar{X}_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i\in[k]}$ (for codes encoding $k$ logical qubits) are obtained by the parities of the basis vectors $\{v_{i}\}$ of $\mathrm{ker}(\partial_{1})$ , which satisfies $f_{i}v_{i}=\bar{X}_{i}$ and $f_{i}^{\prime}v_{i}=\bar{X}_{i}^{\prime}$ (see Def. 24 for details). From the preceding discussion, the effective data error does not trigger any stabilizers in the original data codes $\mathcal{Q}$ and $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ , i.e. $H_{x}a=0$ , $H_{x}^{\prime}c=0$ . This implies that $a$ and $c$ act, with high probability due to the weight bound from local stochasticness, as $Z$ stabilizers on the original data codes, and therefore also commute with the $X$ logical operators of the respective codes, $\langle\bar{X}_{i},a\rangle=0$ . We thus have $\langle f_{1}v_{i},a\rangle=0$ . Taking the adjoint of this inner product, we have $\langle v_{i},f_{1}^{T}a\rangle=0$ . Similarly, we have $\langle v_{i},f_{1}^{\prime T}c\rangle=0$ . Furthermore, since $v_{i}\in\mathrm{ker}(\partial_{1})$ , $\partial_{1}v_{i}=0$ and $\langle\partial_{1}v_{i},b\rangle=0$ . Taking the adjoint, we have $\langle v_{i},\partial_{1}^{T}b\rangle=0$ . Plugging these into Eq. 63, we have that

$$ \langle\left[\tilde{H}_{X}\begin{pmatrix}a\\
b\\
c\end{pmatrix}\right]|_{\mathcal{A}},v_{i}\rangle=\langle f_{1}^{T}a+\partial_{1}^{T}b+f_{1}^{\prime T}c,v_{i}\rangle=0, $$

which indicates that $\partial(e_{1}\oplus e_{2}\oplus\hat{e})|_{\mathcal{A}}$ does not flip the relevant product of stabilizers that product the logical measurement outcomes. Therefore, when using the BSE procedure to perform fault-tolerant lattice surgery with the homological measurement construction, the logical error rate is exponentially suppressed in the code distance.

### S1.6 Numerical simulations

*Figure 14: Circuit for numerically simulating the BSE gadget.*

Here, we present the details of numerically simulating the logical error rates of the BSE gadgets. As illustrated in Fig. 14, given a $[[n,k,d]]$ quantum code $\mathcal{Q}$ and a $[n_{C},k_{C},d_{C}]$ classical code $\mathcal{C}$ , we simulate a circuit on a batch of $k_{C}$ $\mathcal{Q}$ codes that implements a combination of the memory experiment [91] and the stability experiment [92]. Concretely, we initialize the physical qubits of $\mathcal{Q}^{\otimes k_{C}}$ in the product state $\ket{0}^{\otimes n}$ , measure one round of $X$ checks using a BSE gadget associated with $\mathcal{C}$ and one round of $Z$ checks directly, and finally transversally measure them in the $Z$ basis.

As a memory experiment, the logical qubits should all be measured to give logical $+1$ , so we set $k_{C}\times k$ $Z$ logical observables to be the values of the $k_{C}\times k$ logical $Z$ operators of $\mathcal{Q}^{\otimes k_{C}}$ , which are constructed by combinations of the final transversal physical $Z$ measurements. The flip of these $Z$ logical observables characterize the space-like logical errors of the protocol.

Let $H_{X}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{X}\times n}$ be the $X$ check matrix of $\mathcal{Q}$ . We consider $\mathcal{Q}$ with redundant $X$ checks, i.e. $\mathrm{ker}(H_{X}^{T})\neq 0$ . Let $\bm{M}_{X}=\{m_{x,i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{X}}\}$ be a set of basis vectors spanning $\mathrm{ker}(H_{X}^{T})$ , these are the set of “meta X checks” of $\mathcal{Q}$ , each being a product of a subset of $X$ checks indexed by $m_{x,i}$ , that should, in the absence of syndrome errors, have deterministic value $+1$ even if all the constituting $X$ checks are non-deterministic. As such, we have a stability experiment by setting $k_{C}\times|\bm{M}_{X}|$ $X$ logical observables to the values of $\bm{M}_{X}^{\otimes k_{C}}$ , which are constructed by combinations of the $X$ syndromes (extracted using BSE gadget). The flip of these $X$ logical observables characterize the time-like logical errors of the BSE gadget. As a concrete example, taking $\mathcal{Q}$ to be the toric code, we have $\bm{M}_{X}=\{(1,1,\cdots,1)\}$ since the product of all the $X$ checks is $I$ .

The circuit for measuring the $X$ checks using the BSE gadget and how the QEC is performed within the BSE gadget are described in the main text as well as the previous sections. As a concrete example, the circuit using the $[7,4,3]$ Hamming code is shown in Fig. 14.

We note that there is one type of (undetectable) residual error that is not captured by the above numerical experiment: any residual syndrome error on the initial $X$ checks on $\bm{B}_{0}$ that is the boundary of some $Z$ data error $e_{Z}$ will commute with all the logical observables, and thus will not contribute to the reported logical error rates. After fixing the $X$ checks to $+1$ using only the information from the BSE gadget, the prepared state is close to the logical zero states of the underlying quantum code up to $e_{Z}$ . Therefore, these uncaptured errors do affect how far we are from the codespace. Nevertheless, as entailed from the structure of the errors analyzed in Sec. S1.3, there is also some residual $X$ error on $\bm{X}_{0}$ ( $r^{X}$ in Theorem 14), which has essentially the same error mechanisms (it arises from the residual syndrome error on the $Z$ checks on $\bm{A}$ ) as those for $e_{Z}$ and is captured by the numerics here (it anti-commutes with the space-like $Z$ logical observables). As such, the report logical error rates do characterize how far we are from the codespace using the single-shot BSE gadget.

## S2 Batched code switching

Here, we provide the detailed construction of the BCS gadget and prove its fault tolerance.

Given two CSS qLDPC code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ with parameters $[[n_{1},k_{1},d_{1}]]$ and $[[n_{2},k_{2},d_{2}]]$ , respectively. Let $r_{X,i}$ and $r_{Z,i}$ be the rank of the $X$ and $Z$ parity check, respectively, for $\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ (for $i=1,2$ ). According to Def. 6 in the main text, both $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ admit a canonical logical operator basis:

$$ L_{Z}^{i}=\begin{array}[]{ccccc}&\bm{L}_{i}&\bm{Z}_{i}&\bm{X}_{i}\\
&I_{k_{i}}&A_{i}&0&\\
\end{array},\quad L_{X}^{i}=\begin{array}[]{ccccc}&\bm{L}_{i}&\bm{Z}_{i}&\bm{X}_{i}\\
&I_{k_{i}}&0&B_{i}&\\
\end{array}, $$

for $i=1,2$ , where $A_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k_{i}\times r_{X,i}}$ and $B_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k_{i}\times r_{Z,i}}$ . The qubits $[n_{i}]$ are partitioned into three zones with sizes $|\bm{L}_{i}|=k_{i}$ , $|\bm{Z}_{i}|=r_{X,i}$ , and $|\bm{X}_{i}|=r_{Z,i}$ , respectively.

We perform the code switching $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes k_{2}}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ using the following protocol:

- 1. Prepare $r_{X,2}$ (resp. $r_{Z,2}$ ) blocks of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ associated with the $\bm{Z}_{2}$ (resp. $\bm{X}_{2}$ ) zone of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ in logical $\overline{\ket{0}}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ (resp. $\overline{\ket{+}}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ ) using BSE gadgets.

- 2. Measure the stabilizers of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes n_{1}}$ using BSE gadgets.

- 3. Measure transversally the $r_{X,1}$ (resp. $r_{Z,1}$ ) blocks of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ associated with the $\bm{Z}_{1}$ (resp. $\bm{X}_{1}$ ) zone of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ in the $Z$ (rep. $X$ ) basis.

- 4. Apply Pauli feedback on the output $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ block based on the transversal measurement outcomes in step 3 in the following way: Indexing the $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks on the $\bm{L}_{1}$ , $\bm{Z}_{1}$ , and $\bm{X}_{1}$ zones of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ by $[k_{1}]$ , $[r_{Z,1}]$ and $[r_{X,1}]$ , respectively. Apply a classically controlled transversal CNOT between the $i$ -th $\bm{L}_{1}$ block (target) and the $j$ -th $\bm{Z}_{1}$ block (control) if $A_{1}(i,j)=1$ ; Apply a classically controlled transversal CZ between the $i$ -th $\bm{L}_{1}$ block (target) and the $j$ -th $\bm{X}_{1}$ block if $B_{1}(i,j)=1$ .

Now, we prove the fault tolerance of the above protocol. We adopt the standard symplectic representation of the a $n$ -qubit Pauli operator $P\in\mathcal{P}^{n}$ (up to phases) with a vector $(a\mid b)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2n}$ , where $a_{i}=1$ if $Z$ or $Y$ acts on qubit $i$ and $b_{j}=1$ if $X$ or $Y$ acts on qubit $j$ . Let $\mathbf{v}=\{v_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2n}\}$ be a set of vectors, we denote $\langle\mathbf{v}\rangle$ as the group generated by the Pauli operators represented by $\mathbf{v}$ , or equivalently, the subspace of $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2n}$ that is spanned by $\mathbf{v}$ .

We arrange the $n_{1}\times n_{2}$ physical qubits of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes n_{2}}$ (or $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes n_{1}}$ ) on a $[n_{1}]\times[n_{2}]$ rectangle, where $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes n_{2}}$ are defined on the $n_{2}$ columns and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes n_{1}}$ are defined on the $n_{1}$ rows. We denote an operator in the form $(a_{1}\otimes a_{2}\mid 0)$ , where $a_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n_{1}}$ and $a_{2}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n_{2}}$ , as a Pauli $Z$ operator supported on the rectangle $\mathrm{supp}(a_{1})\times\mathrm{supp}(a_{2})$ . Let $\mathbf{a}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{a}_{2}$ be a set of vectors in $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n_{1}}$ and $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n_{2}}$ , respectively, with a slight abuse of notation, we denote $\mathbf{a}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{a}_{2}$ as $\{a_{1}\otimes a_{2}\}_{a_{1}\in\mathbf{a}_{1},a_{2}\in\mathbf{a}_{2}}$ . Given a set of qubits $\bm{R}\subseteq[n_{1}]\times[n_{1}]$ , we denote $\overline{\bm{R}}:=[n_{1}]\times[n_{2}]\backslash\bm{R}$ as complementary set of qubits of $\bm{R}$ , and $l|_{\bm{R}}$ the restriction of an operator $l$ on $\bm{R}$ . We also denote $|l|_{\mathrm{RW}}$ as the row weight of $l$ — the number of rows that $l$ has nonzero support on.

Let $\bm{s}_{z}^{i}$ and $\bm{s}_{x}^{i}$ be the set of $Z$ and $X$ stabilizer generators of $\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ . Let $e_{m}^{n_{i}}$ denote a $n_{i}$ -dimensional unit vector with the $m$ -th entry being $1$ , and $\bm{e}^{n_{i}}:=\{e_{m}^{n_{i}}\}_{m\in[n_{i}]}$ be the set of all unit vectors in $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n_{i}}$ . For ease of notation, we also use $0$ to denote a zero vector or matrix, whose dimension should be clear from the context. The stabilizer group of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes n_{2}}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes n_{1}}$ are given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{1} \displaystyle=\langle(\bm{s}_{z}^{1}\otimes\bm{e}^{n_{2}}\mid 0),(0\mid\mathbf{s}_{x}^{1}\otimes\mathbf{e}^{n_{2}})\rangle, \displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{2} \displaystyle=\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0),(0\mid\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\mathbf{s}_{x}^{2})\rangle, $$

respectively.

Let $\bm{l}_{z}^{i}$ and $\bm{l}_{x}^{i}$ be the canonical logical $Z$ and $X$ operators of $\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ , corresponding to the rows of $L_{Z}^{i}$ and $L_{X}^{i}$ in Eq. (65), respectively. Eq. (65) indicates that we can partition the physical qubits of $\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ , $[n_{i}]$ , into three zones, $[n_{i}]=\bm{L}_{i}\cup\bm{Z}_{i}\cup\bm{X}_{i}$ , where zone $\bm{Z}_{i}$ only supports $\bm{l}_{z}^{i}$ , zone $\bm{X}_{i}$ only supports $\bm{l}_{x}^{i}$ , and zone $\bm{L}_{i}$ supports the intersection of $\bm{l}_{z}^{i}$ and $\bm{l}_{x}^{i}$ . Let $\bm{e}_{L}^{n_{i}}$ , $\bm{e}_{Z}^{n_{i}}$ and $\bm{e}_{X}^{n_{i}}$ denote the set of unit vectors associated with the zone $\bm{L_{i}}$ , $\bm{Z}_{i}$ and $\bm{X}_{i}$ , respectively.

After step 1 of the BCS protocol, the $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ blocks associated with the columns indexed by $\bm{Z}_{2}$ ( $\bm{X}_{2}$ ) are initialized in logical $\overline{\ket{0}}$ (logical $\overline{\ket{+}}$ ). The system is then stabilized by

$$ \mathcal{S}_{o}=\langle(\bm{s}_{z}^{1}\otimes\bm{e}^{n_{2}}\mid 0),(\bm{l}_{z}^{1}\otimes\bm{e}_{Z}^{n_{2}}\mid 0),(0\mid\bm{s}_{x}^{1}\otimes\bm{e}^{n_{2}}),(0\mid\bm{l}_{x}^{1}\otimes\bm{e}_{X}^{n_{2}})\rangle, $$

corresponding to further adding the canonical logical $Z$ ( $X$ ) operators of the $\mathbf{Z}_{2}$ -column ( $\mathbf{X}_{2}$ -column) $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ blocks to $\mathcal{S}_{1}$ . Using the BSE gadget, these stabilizers $\mathcal{S}_{o}$ are deterministically established up to locally stochastical data errors.

After step 3 of the BCS protocol, the encoding is switched to $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes n_{1}}$ with the $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks associated with the rows indexed by $\mathbf{Z}_{1}$ ( $\mathbf{X}_{1}$ ) measured in the $Z$ ( $X$ ) basis. Accordingly, the codes are now stabilized by

$$ \mathcal{S}_{n}=\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0),(\bm{e}_{Z}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{l}_{z}^{2}\mid 0),(0\mid\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{x}^{2}),(0\mid\bm{e}_{X}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{l}_{x}^{2})\rangle, $$

corresponding to further adding the canonical logical $Z$ ( $X$ ) operators of the $\mathbf{Z}_{1}$ -row ( $\mathbf{X}_{2}$ -row) $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks to $\mathcal{S}_{2}$ . Similarly, we also reliably establish these stabilizers $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ up to locally stochastic data errors due to the fault tolerance of the BSE gadget and the transversal $Z$ -( $X$ -)basis measurements.

It remains to prove that we have a large effective code distance during the code deformation process $\mathcal{S}_{o}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{n}$ . According to Ref. [75], this is equivalent to proving that the parent subsystem code of the deformation procedure, defined by the gauge group $\mathcal{G}=\langle\mathcal{S}_{o},\mathcal{S}_{n}\rangle$ , has a distance $\geq\min\{d_{1},d_{2}\}$ .

The subsystem code has stabilizers

$$ \mathcal{S}=Z(\mathcal{G})=\langle(\bm{s}_{z}^{1}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0),(0\mid\bm{s}_{x}^{1}\otimes\bm{s}_{x}^{2})\rangle, $$

which are used to detect and correct errors during the deformation process. $\mathcal{S}$ is LDPC since the stabilizers of both $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ are LDPC. The undetectable logical errors are given by the dressed logical operators of the subsystem code

$$ \bm{L}_{d}=C(\mathcal{S})\backslash\mathcal{G}. $$

Equivalently, they are given by the bare logical operators

$$ \bm{L}_{b}=C(\mathcal{G})\backslash\mathcal{S}=\langle(\bm{l}_{z}^{1}\otimes\bm{l}_{z}^{2}\mid 0),(0\mid\bm{l}_{x}^{1}\otimes\bm{l}_{x}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle\backslash(0\mid 0), $$

multiplied by the gauge operators in $\mathcal{G}$ .

Since the code is CSS, it suffices to prove its $Z$ distance (the proof for the $X$ distance follows). Since a bare logical $Z$ operator $l^{b}_{z}\in\bm{L}_{b}$ can be viewed either as a set of column vectors each being a logical operator in $\bm{l}^{1}_{Z}$ or a set of row vectors each being a logical operator in $\bm{l}^{2}_{Z}$ , we have $|l^{b}_{z}|\geq\max\{d_{1},d_{2}\}$ . Thus, it remains to prove that any bare $Z$ logical operator cannot be weight reduced below $\min\{d_{1},d_{2}\}$ by the $Z$ gauge operators in $\mathcal{G}$ .

Let $v_{0}=(0\mid 0)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2n}$ denote the zero vector. Let $l_{z}^{b}\in\langle(\bm{l}_{z}^{1}\otimes\bm{l}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle\backslash v_{0}$ be a nontrivial bare logical $Z$ operator, $s_{z}\in\langle(\bm{s}_{z}^{1}\otimes\bm{e}^{n_{2}}\mid 0)\rangle$ a $Z$ stabilizer of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes n_{2}}$ or $v_{0}$ , $l_{z}\in\langle(\bm{l}_{z}^{1}\otimes\bm{e}_{Z}^{n_{2}}\mid 0)\rangle$ a logical $Z$ operator of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes r_{X,2}}$ or $v_{0}$ , $s_{z}^{\prime}\in(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)$ a $Z$ stabilizer of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes n_{1}}$ or $v_{0}$ , and $l_{z}^{\prime}\in$ a $Z$ logical operator $(\bm{e}_{Z}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{l}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)$ of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes r_{X,1}}$ or $v_{0}$ . We aim to prove that

$$ |l_{z}^{b}+l_{z}+s_{z}+l_{z}^{\prime}+s_{z}^{\prime}|\geq\min\{d_{1},d_{2}\}. $$

.

We prove this by contradiction. Assume that $|l_{z}^{b}+l_{z}+s_{z}+l_{z}^{\prime}+s_{z}^{\prime}|<d_{1}$ and $|l_{z}^{b}+l_{z}+s_{z}+l_{z}^{\prime}+s_{z}^{\prime}|<d_{2}$ .

First, we consider the case where $l_{z}\neq v_{0}$ , and show how this leads to $|l_{z}^{b}+l_{z}+s_{z}+l_{z}^{\prime}+s_{z}^{\prime}|\geq d_{1}$ , which causes a contradiction. In this case, there exists a column $q\in\bm{Z}_{2}$ such that $l_{z}$ has a component $(l_{z}^{1}\otimes e_{q})$ , where $l_{z}^{1}$ is a nontrivial logical operator in $\bm{l}^{1}_{z}$ .

To simplify the proof, we first define the “reduced weight” of an operator $l$ with respect to $\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0),(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{l}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle$ :

$$ |l|^{r}:=\min_{v_{z}^{\prime}\in\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0),(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{l}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle}|l+v_{z}^{\prime}|, $$

which is the minimum weight of $l$ modulo all possible $Z$ stabilizers and $Z$ logical operators of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes n_{1}}$ . We then have

$$ |l_{z}^{b}+l_{z}+s_{z}+l_{z}^{\prime}+s_{z}^{\prime}|\geq|l_{z}^{b}+l_{z}+s_{z}|^{r}. $$

The reduced weight has a property $|l+l^{\prime}|^{r}=|l|^{r}$ if $|l^{\prime}|^{r}=0$ . Therefore, we further have

$$ |l_{z}^{b}+l_{z}+s_{z}+l_{z}^{\prime}+s_{z}^{\prime}|\geq|l_{z}+s_{z}|^{r}, $$

since $|l_{z}^{b}|^{r}=0$ .

Now, we prove the following fact: Let $\bm{R}:=[n_{1}]\times\bm{Z}_{2}$ , then for any operator $l$ that is supported only on $\bm{R}$ , we have $|l|^{r}\geq|l|_{\mathrm{RW}}$ . To see this, we utilize the canonical form of the stabilizers of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ . Analogous to Eq. (65), we can find a basis of the stabilizers of $\mathcal{Q}_{i}$ [74]

$$ S_{Z}^{i}=\begin{array}[]{ccccc}&\bm{L}_{i}&\bm{Z}_{i}&\bm{X}_{i}\\
&B_{i}^{T}&C_{i}&I&\\
\end{array},\quad S_{X}^{i}=\begin{array}[]{ccccc}&\bm{L}_{i}&\bm{Z}_{i}&\bm{X}_{i}\\
&A_{i}^{T}&I&D_{i}&\\
\end{array}, $$

whose rows correspond to $\bm{s}_{z}^{i}$ and $\bm{s}_{x}^{i}$ , respectively. According to Eq. (76), $S_{X}^{2}$ takes a form of $I$ on $\bm{Z}_{2}$ , indicating that $\langle\bm{e}_{Z}^{n_{2}}\rangle$ is not in the kernel of $S^{2}_{X}$ . Then, for any row vector $v=(e_{i}^{n_{1}}\otimes v_{2}\mid 0)$ (for some $i$ ), where $v_{2}$ has and only has nontrivial support on $\bm{Z}_{2}$ , $v$ is not equivalent to some vector in $\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0),(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{l}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle$ (which would be in the kernel of $S^{2}_{X}$ ) and therefore, $|v|^{r}>0$ . This indicates that, for any operator $l$ supported only on $\bm{R}$ , which can be viewed as a set of row vectors each supported only on $\bm{Z}_{2}$ and not eliminable by $\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0),(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{l}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle$ , its weight cannot be reduced below its row weight.

Note that in Eq. (75), $l_{z}$ is already supported on $\mathbf{R}$ . We now aim to move $s_{z}$ also to $\bm{R}$ by adding an operator $v_{z}\in\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0),(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{l}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle$ , and show that $|l_{z}+s_{z}|^{r}=|l_{z}+(s_{z}+v_{z})|^{r}\geq|l_{z}+(s_{z}+v_{z})|_{\mathrm{RW}}\geq d_{1}$ . To do this, we first clean out the support of $s_{z}$ on $[n_{1}]\times\bm{X}_{2}$ by applying some stabilizer $s_{z,0}\in\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle$ (this utilizes the canonical form of $S^{2}_{Z}$ in Eq. (76), which acts as $I$ on $\bm{X}_{2}$ ). Now, $s_{z}+s_{z,0}$ is supported only on $[n_{1}]\times(\bm{L}_{2}\cup\bm{Z}_{2})$ . We can further clean out its support on $[n_{1}]\times\bm{L}_{2}$ by adding another operator $l_{z,0}\in(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{l}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle$ (this utilizes the canonical form of $L^{2}_{Z}$ in Eq. (65), which has an $I$ on $\bm{L}_{2}$ ). Denote $s_{z}+s_{z,0}+l_{z,0}$ as $s_{z,R}$ , which only supports on $\bm{R}$ . We can achieve this in a way that $s_{z,R}$ is still a set of column vectors each being a stabilizer of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ since each stabilizer generator $s_{z}^{1}\otimes e^{n_{2}}_{j}$ of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes n_{2}}$ on a column $j$ can be cleaned to an operator in the form $s_{z}^{1}\otimes v_{R}$ for some $v_{R}$ supported only on $\bm{Z}_{2}$ . Now, we have

$$ |l_{z}+s_{z}|^{r}=|l_{z}+s_{z,R}|^{r}\geq|l_{z}+s_{z,R}|_{\mathrm{RW}}\geq d_{1}, $$

where the last equality utilizes that $l_{z}+s_{z,R}$ contains at least a column of nontrivial operator of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ . This contradicts the assumption and thus $l_{z}$ must be $v_{0}$ .

By symmetry, we must have $l_{z}^{\prime}=v_{0}$ , too. Therefore, it remains to analyze the case when $l_{z}=l_{z}^{\prime}=v_{0}$ . In this case, we aim to show that

$$ |l^{b}_{z}+s_{z}+s_{z}^{\prime}|\geq d_{1}, $$

yet contradicting the assumption. To this end, we define another reduced weight of an operator $l$ with respect to $\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)$

$$ |l|^{r^{\prime}}:=\min_{v_{z}^{\prime}\in\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle}|l+v_{z}^{\prime}|, $$

which is the minimum weight of $l$ modulo the $Z$ stabilizers of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes n_{1}}$ . We now aim to prove that $|l^{b}_{z}+s_{z}|^{r^{\prime}}\geq d_{1}$ . Similar to the previous arguments, we have the following fact: for any operator $l$ supported only on $\bm{R}^{\prime}:=[n_{1}]\times(\bm{L}_{2}\cup\bm{Z}_{2})$ , we have $|l|^{r^{\prime}}\geq|l|_{\mathrm{RW}}$ . Again, we can clean $s_{z}$ to $\bm{R}^{\prime}$ by adding an operator $s_{z,0}\in\langle(\bm{e}^{n_{1}}\otimes\bm{s}_{z}^{2}\mid 0)\rangle$ while having that $s_{z,R^{\prime}}:=s_{z}+s_{z,0}$ is still a $Z$ stabilizer of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes n_{2}}$ . Then,

$$ |l^{b}_{z}+s_{z}+s_{z}^{\prime}|\geq|l^{b}_{z}+s_{z}|^{r^{\prime}}=|l^{b}_{z}+s_{z,R^{\prime}}|^{r^{\prime}}\geq d_{1}, $$

which contradicts the assumption.

Based on the above analysis, we conclude that $|l_{z}^{b}+l_{z}+s_{z}+l_{z}^{\prime}+s_{z}^{\prime}|\geq\min\{d_{1},d_{2}\}$ , and thus the distance of the subsystem code is at least $\min\{d_{1},d_{2}\}$ .

Finally, we bound the logical error rate of the BCS gadget using the standard percolation analysis in Ref. [1]. Since the entire protocol remains LDPC and has a large effective distance $\Omega(\min\{{d_{1},d_{2}}\})$ , we can bound the logical error rate by

$$ \mathcal{O}\left(n_{1}n_{2}(p/p_{\mathrm{th}})^{\Omega(\min\{{d_{1},d_{2}}\})}\right), $$

according to Eq.(3) of Ref. [1].

### S2.1 Reducing Overhead Constant Factors with Hypergraph Product Codes

In this section, we describe how the qubit overhead for performing batched code switching can be further reduced. While the general procedure described above achieves constant overhead, for $k_{1}k_{2}$ logical qubits, it still requires $n\sim n_{1}n_{2}/r_{c}$ qubits, where $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ are the block lengths of the quantum code and $r_{c}$ is the encoding rate of the classical code used in BSE. In practice, the classical code can achieve fairly high rate using modest batch size, but the quantum codes often achieve a rate of only a few percent, leading to significant overhead. We now show how utilizing additional structure of hypergraph (HGP) codes, the same procedure can be performed using $n\sim(n_{1}+n_{2})/r_{c}$ qubits, representing a sizable reduction for large $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ . Thus, instead of a multiplicative, the overhead is now additive, alleviating the qubit requirements.

We first consider the qubit requirements for the standard BCS gadget described above, when switching from $k_{2}$ copies of a $[[n_{1},k_{1},d_{1}]]$ quantum code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ to $k_{1}$ copies of a $[[n_{2},k_{2},d_{2}]]$ quantum code $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ . As shown in the main text, the protocol involves growing the code into a joint $n_{1}n_{2}$ -qubit intermediate code.

In the protocol, we use a BCS gadget to perform a round of reliable syndrome measurement. The largest instantaneous qubit usage occurs when performing syndrome measurements on the joint intermediate code. In particular, we will need to perform syndrome measurements on $n_{1}$ copies of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ in parallel. To do so, we can use a $[n_{1}/r_{c},n_{1},d]$ classical code and a BSE gadget, resulting in a total of $(2/r_{c}-1)n_{1}n_{2}$ data qubits for $k_{1}k_{2}$ logical qubits. While this is a constant, the prefactor is somewhat large, as the number of qubits is multiplied between the two codes.

We now describe how we can utilize the structure of certain quantum codes, such as HGP codes, to reduce this overhead. The key idea is to utilize homomorphic measurement gadgets to perform row-wise and column-wise switching separately, leading to an overhead that scales as the sum instead of product of the individual codes, reducing the costs.

More specifically, let $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ be the HGP of classical codes $[n_{a1},k_{a1},d]\times[n_{b1},k_{b1},d]$ , and let $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ be the HGP of classical codes $[n_{a2},k_{a2},d]\times[n_{b2},k_{b2},d]$ . We assume that the dual code of the classical codes contain no logical qubits. We perform code switching in two steps: We start with $k_{2}=k_{a2}k_{b2}$ copies of $[n_{a1},k_{a1},d]\times[n_{b1},k_{b1},d]$ , switch into $k_{a1}k_{b2}$ copies of $[n_{a2},k_{a2},d]\times[n_{b1},k_{b1},d]$ , and finally switch into $k_{1}=k_{a1}k_{b1}$ copies of $[n_{a2},k_{a2},d]\times[n_{b2},k_{b2},d]$ . This corresponds to first performing switching along the rows, and then the columns.

We now explain how to perform the switching along the rows, and estimate its overhead. The column switching can be done similarly. Let $A$ be the code with parameters $[n_{a1}k_{a2}+n_{a2}k_{a1},2k_{a1}k_{a2},d]$ formed by appending $k_{a2}$ copies of $[n_{a1},k_{a1},d]$ and $k_{a1}$ copies of $[n_{a2},k_{a2},d]$ . We perform a homomorphic logical measurement on the code $A\times[n_{b1},k_{b1},d]$ , with added ancilla qubits so that in the horizontal direction, a logical $ZZ$ measurement is performed between the $i$ th qubit in the $j$ th copy of $[n_{a1},k_{a1},d]$ and the $j$ th qubit in the $i$ th copy of $[n_{a2},k_{a2},d]$ . Following the transversal $X$ -basis measurement of the $[n_{a1},k_{a1},d]$ blocks, this allows the fault-tolerant teleportation of information to the intermediate code, as long as the homomorphic logical measurement is performed fault-tolerantly. We can perform the homomorphic logical measurements using BSE gadgets, and the fact that we have $k_{b2}$ copies in the vertical direction naturally provides a suitable batch size: we can just use a $[n_{b2},k_{b2},d]$ classical code, although since there are fewer requirements on this code, more efficient choices will likely exist.

The total number of data qubits required in the above steps can be estimated as follows: we require $(n_{a1}k_{a2}+n_{a2}k_{a1}+k_{a1}k_{a2})n_{b1}$ qubits for each code. Denoting the rate of the classical code used in the BSE gadget as $r_{c}^{\prime}$ , we will require $(2/r_{c}^{\prime}-1)k_{b2}$ copies in the vertical direction. If we assume $n_{a1}=n_{b1}=\sqrt{n_{1}}$ and $n_{a2}=n_{b2}=\sqrt{n_{2}}$ for simplicity, then the number of data qubits required can be simplified to $n\sim(2/r_{c}^{\prime}-1)\sqrt{n_{1}k_{2}}\quantity(\sqrt{n_1k_2}+\sqrt{n_2k_1}+\sqrt{k_1k_2})$ , which is approximately $(2/r_{c}^{\prime}-1)\cdot 2nk$ when the code parameters are equal. Thus, compared to the general BCS construction, we can reduce the overhead by a factor of $n/k$ , corresponding to the encoding rate of an individual quantum code.

## S3 Batched addressable Cliffords

Here, we prove Theorem 3 of the main text by explicitly constructing the batched addressable Clifford (BAC) gadgets for any $[[n_{1},k_{1},d_{1}]]$ CSS qLDPC code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ . Concretely, we present a scheme that implements any $k_{1}$ -qubit Clifford circuit $C_{k}$ on a batch of $k_{2}=\Omega(d_{1}^{2})$ $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ blocks using at most $\mathcal{O}(k_{2})$ ancillary $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ blocks (therefore, with a constant space overhead) and in a depth of at most $\mathcal{O}\left(D_{P}(C_{k})\right)$ , where $D_{P}(C_{k})$ denotes the depth of implementing $C_{k}$ with physical circuits.

As discussed in the main text, we can decompose $C_{k}$ into layers of circuits each consisting of only $H$ , $S$ , or CNOT gates with a constant overhead. Thus, we present the implementation of $C_{k}$ of these three gate types separately. Let $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ be a symmetric HGP code (i.e. the two base classical codes of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ are identical, good classical LDPC codes) with parameters $[[n_{2}=\Theta(k_{2}),k_{2},d_{2}=\Theta(\sqrt{k_{2}})\geq d_{1}]]$ . The general strategy is to code switch from $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ to $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ using a BCS gadget, perform transversal Clifford gates on $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ , and code switch back to $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ using another BCS gadget.

First, we present the implementation of a $k_{1}$ -qubit CNOT circuit $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}$ on $k_{2}$ blocks of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ , i.e. $\overline{C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ . $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}$ can be decomposed into $D_{P}$ layers of physical CNOTs, $C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}=\prod_{t=1}^{D_{P}}(\bigotimes_{m}\mathrm{CNOT(p^{(t)}_{m},q^{(t)}_{m})})$ , where $\{(p^{(t)}_{m},q^{(t)}_{m})\}$ index pairs of qubits that each physical CNOT gate is acting on, which are distinct for different $m$ at the same time step $t$ . Let $\bar{Q}_{i,j}$ be the $i$ -th logical qubit of the $j$ -th $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ block. We first switch from $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ to $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ using the BCS gadget. This routes $\bar{Q}_{i,j}$ to the $j$ -th logical qubit of the $i$ -th $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ block. We then implement $D_{P}$ layers of transversal CNOTs on the $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks, where the $t$ -th layer consists of the following: for each $m$ , apply a transversal CNOT between the $p^{(t)}_{m}$ -th $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ block and the $q^{(t)}_{m}$ -th $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ block. These transversal CNOT gates then implement the desired logical circuit, $\overline{C_{\mathrm{CNOT}}}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ , via $\prod_{t=1}^{D_{P}}\bigotimes_{j\in[k_{2}]}\bigotimes_{m}\overline{\mathrm{CNOT}}(\bar{Q}_{p_{m}^{(t)},j},\bar{Q}_{q_{m}^{(t)},j})$ . Finally, we switch back to $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ again using the BCS gadget. Clearly, the entire protocol involves only $\mathcal{O}(n_{2})=\mathcal{O}(k_{2})$ blocks of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ . In addition, since each of the BCS gadget has a depth $\mathcal{O}(1)$ and the transversal CNOTs (interleaved with syndrome extractions on $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ ) have a depth $\mathcal{O}(D_{P})$ , the protocol has a depth $\mathcal{O}(D_{P})$ .

Second, we implement a $k_{1}$ -qubit $H$ circuit $C_{H}$ on $k_{2}$ blocks of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ , i.e. $\overline{C_{H}}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ . Any $C_{H}=\bigotimes_{m\in\mathbf{\Lambda}\subseteq[k_{1}]}H(m)$ , which applies $H$ to a subset $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ of the $k_{1}$ qubits, can be implemented with a physical depth $1$ . Therefore, we aim to implement $\overline{C_{H}}^{\otimes k_{2}}=\bigotimes_{j\in[k_{2}]}\bigotimes_{m\in\mathbf{\Lambda}}\bar{H}(\bar{Q}_{m,j})$ with a constant depth. We start, again, by switching to $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ using the BCS gadget. Then, we apply the fold-transversal $H-\mathrm{SWAP}$ gates [42] on a subset of the $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks indexed by $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ . This implements the following gates:

$$ \bigotimes_{m\in\mathbf{\Lambda}}\left(\bigotimes_{j\in[k_{2}]}\bar{H}(\bar{Q}_{m,j})\bigotimes_{\alpha}\overline{\mathrm{SWAP}}(\bar{Q}_{m,p_{\alpha}},\bar{Q}_{m,q_{\alpha}})\right), $$

where $\{p_{\alpha},q_{\alpha}\}$ index pairs of logical qubits of $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ that are mirrored along the diagonal, i.e. $\{(i,j),(j,i)\}_{i\neq j}$ . These implements the desired gates $\overline{C_{H}}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ up to some extra SWAP operations within each $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ , which are the same across all the $|\mathbf{\Lambda}|$ $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks. Let $\mathrm{SWAP}^{\prime}$ denote the $k_{2}$ -qubit SWAP circuit on each $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ block in Eq. (82), the extra swap operations are simply $\overline{\mathrm{SWAP^{\prime}}}^{\otimes|\mathbf{\Lambda}|}$ being applied to the $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ subset of the $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks, where the encoded gates are with respect to the $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ encoding. We can then cancel these extra swap operations by introducing $k_{1}-|\mathbf{\Lambda}|$ dummy $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks, applying the batched SWAP gates $\overline{\mathrm{SWAP}}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ in a similar way as to implement the batched CNOT circuits described above – switching from $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ to $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ , swapping the $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ blocks according to $\mathrm{SWAP}^{\prime}$ , and switching back to $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ . After cancelling these extra swap operations, we have implemented the desired $\overline{C_{H}}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ . Finally, we switch back to $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ using another BCS gadget. Clearly, the entire protocol involves only $\mathcal{O}(n_{2})=\mathcal{O}(k_{2})$ $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ blocks and has a constant depth (since the intermediate SWAP circuit has a constant depth).

Finally, we implement a $k_{1}$ -qubit $S$ circuit $C_{S}$ on $k_{2}$ blocks of $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ , i.e. $\overline{C_{S}}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ . Same as a $H$ circuit, any $C_{S}=\bigotimes_{m\in\mathbf{\Lambda}\subseteq[k_{1}]}S(m)$ , which applies $S$ to a subset $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ of the $k_{1}$ qubits, can be implemented with a physical depth $1$ . Therefore, we aim to implement $\overline{C_{S}}^{\otimes k_{2}}=\bigotimes_{j\in[k_{2}]}\bigotimes_{m\in\mathbf{\Lambda}}\bar{S}(\bar{Q}_{m,j})$ with a constant depth. Again, we can implement $\overline{C_{S}}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ by switching to $\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{\otimes k_{1}}$ , applying global $\bar{S}$ gates on a subset of the $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks indexed by $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ , and then switching back to $\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ . The main challenge is then to implement $\overline{S}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ for some $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks with a low space-time overhead. We implement such global $S$ gates using the gate teleportation circuit in Fig. 15 that consumes a $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ block of $\overline{\ket{i}}^{\otimes k_{2}}$ states. To have sufficient copies of $\overline{\ket{i}}$ states, we first prepare one block of $\overline{\ket{i}}$ states with some space overhead $W(k_{2})$ and time overhead $T(k_{2})$ , and then catalyze more blocks of $\overline{\ket{i}}$ states using the circuit in Fig. 15(b). Note that the global $H$ gates on a $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ block in Fig. 15(b) can be implemented efficiently using the batched $H$ gadget described above and the global $CZ$ gates between two $\mathcal{Q}_{2}$ blocks can be implemented by conjugating a transversal CNOT with two batched global $H$ gates. As the catalyst circuit and the $S$ -teleportation circuit can all be implemented with a constant space overhead and in a constant depth, the average space-time overhead over $D$ uses of the batched $S$ gadget is constant if the initial preparation of a block of $\overline{\ket{i}}$ states has a space overhead $W(k_{2})=\mathcal{O}(k_{2})$ and $T(k_{2})=\mathrm{O}(D)$ . Using, e.g. the protocol in Ref. [16], we can achieve $W(k_{2})=\mathcal{O}(1)$ and $T(k_{2})=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{k_{2}})$ . Therefore, we achieve a constant space-time overhead on average for any logical circuits that apply $D=\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{k_{2}})$ batched $S$ gadgets.

## S4 Parallel non-Clifford gates via distilled $T$ measurements

*Figure 16: Distillation of $T$ measurement. (a) Implementation of a global noisy $T$ gate on a $[[n_{1},k_{1},d_{1}]]$ CSS code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ with a bounded marginal error rate $p_{0}$ using faulty $T$ measurements on an ancilla $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ code. The faulty $T$ measurements can be implemented by code switching to $k_{1}$ $[[n_{3},1,d_{3}]]$ 3D color codes (indicated by the green lines) using the BCS gadget. Following the $T$ measurements, only random Pauli fixups are needed on the data $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ code. (b) Implementation of a lower-error-rate global $T$ gate on the $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ code by distilling a higher-fidelity $T$ measurement on the ancilla code utilizing a $[[n_{D},1,d_{D}]]$ distillation code $\mathcal{Q}_{D}$ from many copies of the noisy $T$ measurements in (a).*

Here, we present a scheme that distills higher-fidelity $T$ measurements from lower-fidelity ones.

As shown in Fig. 16(a), given a $[[n_{1},k_{1},d_{1}]]$ CSS qLDPC code $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ , we can perform noisy global $T$ gates on $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ by coupling it to an ancilla $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ code, performing a faulty $T$ measurement [49] on the ancilla code, and applying feedback $Z$ corrections on the data code. As presented in the main text, the faulty $T$ measurements on the ancilla code can be implemented by switching to $k_{1}$ copies of $[[n_{3},1,d_{3}]]$ 3D color codes using the BCS gadget and then performing the $T$ measurements on the color codes. By choosing $d_{3}=\mathcal{O}(\log n_{1})$ , these $T$ measurements have a marginal error rate $p_{0}$ that is independent of $n_{1}$ . Consequently, the noisy global $T$ gates on $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ have a bounded marginal error rate $p_{0}$ . Crucially, by implementing the $T$ gates using $T$ measurements instead of $|T\rangle$ states, we avoid the Clifford fixups on the data $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ code (instead, we only have Pauli fixups), which could induce a large compilation overhead when implementing them with the BAC gadget.

In Fig. 16(b), we show how to obtain lower-error-rate $T$ measurements on $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ by consuming many copies of the noisy $T$ measurements in Fig. 16(a). The idea is to replace the faulty $T$ measurement on the ancilla code in Fig. 16(a) with an error-corrected $T$ measurement using a “distillation” code $\mathcal{Q}_{D}$ . Without loss of generality, we assume that $\mathcal{Q}_{D}$ only encodes $1$ logical qubit and has parameters $[[n_{D},1,d_{D}]]$ . In addition, it supports a transversal $T$ gate. Then, we perform the distillation following the protocol in Ref. [50]: (1) prepare $n_{D}-1$ extra $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ codes in either logical $0$ or $+$ , (2) perform an encoding circuit $\mathcal{E}$ that encodes the ancilla $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ code into the concatenated code with the outer code being $\mathcal{Q}_{D}$ (e.g. by using the measurement-based encoding protocol in Def. 6 of the main text), (3) apply the transversal $T$ gate on $\mathcal{Q}_{D}$ , where each $T$ gate on a $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ block is implemented using the noisy $T$ measurement scheme in Fig. 16(a), (4) perform a round of syndrome extraction for the $\mathcal{Q}_{D}$ code to correct the errors associated with the preceding noisy $T$ gates on $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ , (5) apply a decoding circuit $\mathcal{E}^{-1}$ (using e.g. the measurement-based decoding protocol in Def. 6 of the main text) that decodes back into the ancilla $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ code, (6) perform a transversal $X$ measurement on the ancilla $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ code. In the regime where $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ is large, the only errors of the above protocol come from the noisy $T$ measurements on the $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ codes, which have a bounded error rate $p_{0}$ . As such, the final $T$ gates in Fig. 16(b) have a marginal error rate $\mathcal{O}\left(p_{0}^{(d_{D}+1)/2}\right)$ . For instance, using a $[[15,1,3]]$ quantum Reed-Muller code, we can suppress the error to $\mathcal{O}(p_{0}^{2})$ . By induction, we can implement global $T$ gates on $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ with lower and lower error rates by concatenating the above distillation scheme and implementing a multi-level distillation. Crucially, we only need random Pauli fixups on $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ codes as opposed to Clifford fixups throughout the protocol, and thus do not introduce extra compilation overhead.

Finally, using high-rate distillation codes in Ref. [17], we can distill $T$ gates $\mathcal{Q}_{1}$ codes in batches with a space-time overhead $k_{1}^{o(1)}$ , where $o(1)\sim 1/\log\log k_{1}$ .

Here, we detail the magic state cultivation/teleportation protocols for the self-dual BB codes in Table I of the main text.

In Sec. S5.1, we present the details of the merged color-surface-BB code, where the cultivated magic states are eventually encoded in. In particular, we prove that it has a distance lower bounded by the distance of the BB code. In Sec. S5.2, we detail the protocol that merges small color codes with a BB code into the final color-surface-BB code and analyze its logical error rates. In Sec. S5.3, we show how to couple the merged color-surface-BB code with a standard BB code using a homomorphic CNOT, which is a variant of the standard transversal CNOT. In Sec. S5.4, we show how to implement the logical translation gadget for a BB code, which is utilized in the main text for simulating lattice Hamiltonians. Finally, in Sec. S5.5, we describe how to perform the Clifford fixups in the $T$ -teleportation circuit in Fig. 6(c) of the main text.

$$ \tilde{H}_{X}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}H_{x}&0&0\\
f_{1}^{T}&\partial_{1}^{T}&f_{1}^{\prime T}\\
0&0&H_{x}^{\prime}\\
\end{array}\right),\quad\tilde{H}_{Z}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}H_{z}&f_{0}&0\\
0&\partial_{0}&0\\
0&f_{0}^{\prime}&H_{z}^{\prime}\\
\end{array}\right). $$

Let $\{\bar{X}_{i}\in Q_{1}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ and $\{\bar{X}_{i}^{\prime}\in Q_{1}^{\prime}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ be a basis for the first homological group of $\mathcal{Q}$ and $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ , respectively. Both $f_{1}$ and $f_{1}^{\prime}$ have a maximum row- and column-weight of $1$ and there exists a basis $\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ for $\mathrm{ker}(\partial_{1})$ that satisfies

$$ f_{1}v_{i}=\bar{X}_{i},\quad f_{1}^{\prime}v_{i}=\bar{X}_{i}^{\prime}, $$

for $i\in[k]$ . We denote the merged code as $\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}(\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{Q}^{\prime},\mathcal{A})$ .

The above protocol can be viewed as merging the two codes $\mathcal{Q}$ and $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ through $k$ parallel lattice-surgery logical measurements, $\{\bar{X}_{i}\bar{X}^{\prime}_{i}\}_{i\in[k]}$ , which are obtained by measuring the new added $X$ checks in $A_{1}$ .

Now, we describe how to construct the merged color-surface-BB code using the gadget in Def. 24.

Let $H_{\mathrm{rep}}(n)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{(n-1)\times n}$ denotes the standard repetition-code check matrix with $n$ bits and $n-1$ checks, and $H_{\mathrm{cyc}}(P,n)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n\times n}$ , where $P\in\mathbb{F}_{2}(z)/(z^{n}-1)$ a cyclic matrix with a generator $P$ represented by a polynomial in $z$ . Note that $H_{\mathrm{rep}}(n)$ corresponds to $H_{\mathrm{cyc}}(1+z,n)$ without the periodical boundary condition.

Given a $[[n_{c},1,d_{c}]]$ color code $\mathcal{Q}_{C}$ and a $[[n_{s},1,d^{\prime}_{s,X}=d_{c},d^{\prime}_{s,Z}]]$ rotated surface code $\mathcal{Q}_{S}$ , we construct a repetition-code adapter $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{C-S}}$ with $A_{-1}=0$ and $\partial_{1}=H_{\mathrm{rep}}(d_{c})$ . The $d_{c}$ $X$ checks in $A_{1}$ are connected transversally to the weight- $d_{c}$ boundary logical $X$ operators of $\mathcal{Q}_{C}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{S}$ ( $f_{1}$ and $f_{1}^{\prime}$ take the form of the identity matrix when restricted to the support of the logical operators), respectively. Let $(\bar{X}_{C},\bar{Z}_{C})$ and $(\bar{X}_{S},\bar{Z}_{S})$ be the logical operators of $\mathcal{Q}_{C}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{S}$ , respectively. The merged code $\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}(\mathcal{Q}_{C},\mathcal{Q}_{S},\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{C-S}})$ is merged through a $\bar{X}_{C}\bar{X}_{S}$ lattice-surgery measurement. In our case, we take the merged color-surface code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ as the dual of $\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}(\mathcal{Q}_{C},\mathcal{Q}_{S},\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{C-S}})$ , i.e. by swapping the $X$ and $Z$ checks in $\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}(\mathcal{Q}_{C},\mathcal{Q}_{S},\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{C-S}})$ , which is equivalent to merging $\mathcal{Q}_{C}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{S}$ through a $\bar{Z}_{C}\bar{Z}_{S}$ measurement. As proved in Lemma 27, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ has a $Z$ distance matching that of the color code $d_{c}$ and a boosted $X$ distance $d_{c}+d_{s,X}$ , where $d_{s,X}=d^{\prime}_{s,Z}$ is the $Z$ distance of $\mathcal{Q}_{S}$ . We illustrate the adapter $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{C-S}}$ for $d_{c}=3$ with the purple strip in Fig. 17. Note that this adapter construction is identical to that in Ref. [96].

Next, we merge $k_{b}$ copies of the color-surface code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ with a $[[n_{b},k_{b},d_{b}]]$ BB code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ . To obtain a merged code with distance $\geq d_{b}$ (which will be proved later), we choose the $X$ distance of the thin surface code such that $d_{c}+d_{s,X}\geq d_{b}$ . We then merge $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ with $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ through an adapter $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}$ described in the following: $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}$ consists of $k_{b}$ disjoint and identical copies $\{\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{k_{b}}$ , where each $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(i)}$ couples to the $X$ logical operator of the $i$ -th logical qubit in $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ and the $X$ logical operator of a copy of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ . In other words,

$$ \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}=\tilde{Q}(\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}},\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}^{\otimes k_{b}},\bigotimes_{i=1}^{k_{b}}\mathcal{A}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}). $$

We illustrate $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ , which couples to the first logical operator $\bar{X}_{U,1}$ in the $U$ block of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ , with the orange strip in Fig. 17. $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ is simply taken as the gauging ancilla system for measuring $\bar{X}_{U,1}$ , which is constructed in Ref. [14]. Here, we briefly describe the construction and refer technical readers to Ref. [14] for more details.

We construct $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}:A_{1}\xrightarrow{\partial_{1}}A_{0}\xrightarrow{\partial_{0}}A_{-1}$ using a graph $G(V,E)$ , where the vertices $V$ and the edges $E$ are associated with basis elements of $A_{1}$ ( $X$ checks) and $A_{0}$ (qubits), respectively, and a cycle basis of $G$ are associated with the basis elements of $A_{-1}$ ( $Z$ checks). We introduce a vertex for each qubit in the support of $\bar{X}_{U,1}$ , thus $|V|=|\bar{X}_{U,1}|=l$ for a $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}=\mathrm{BB}(c,d;R_{l,m})$ code. This gives a bijection $\tau:\mathrm{supp}(\bar{X}_{U,1})\rightarrow V$ . Then, for each $Z$ check $s_{Z}$ that has a nontrivial support $s_{Z}|_{\mathrm{supp}(\bar{X}_{U,1})}$ on $\mathrm{supp}(\bar{X}_{U,1})$ , add $|s_{Z}|_{\mathrm{supp}(\bar{X}_{U,1})}|/2$ edges that give a perfect matching of $\tau(s_{Z}|_{\mathrm{supp}(\bar{X}_{U,1})})$ to $E$ . In our case, for the special BB codes in Table I of the main text with the same polynomail $c=1+y^{3}+x(y^{2}+y^{4})$ , there are $2l$ $Z$ checks with non-trivial support on $\mathrm{supp}(\bar{X}_{U,1})$ , all of weight $2$ . Thus, $E$ with $|E|=2l$ simply consists of all edges associated with $\{\tau(s_{Z}|_{\mathrm{supp}(\bar{X}_{U,1})})\}$ . Moreover, $\partial_{1}$ , which is given by the edge-vertex adjacency matrix of $G$ , takes the following form:

$$ \partial_{1}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}H_{\mathrm{cyc}}(1+z^{3},l)\\
H_{\mathrm{cyc}}(z^{2}+z^{4},l)\\
\end{array}\right), $$

with two sets of checks associated with the rows of $H_{\mathrm{cyc}}(1+z^{3},l)$ and $H_{\mathrm{cyc}}(z^{2}+z^{4},l)$ , respectively. Equivalently, we can write Eq. (87) as

$$ \partial_{1}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}H_{\mathrm{cyc}}(1+z,l)\\
H_{\mathrm{cyc}}(1+z^{\beta},l)\\
\end{array}\right), $$

where $\beta$ depends on $l$ , by permuting the bits and the checks. For instance, we have $\beta=3$ for the $[[66,6,8]]$ -code with $l=11$ . In fact, we can equivalently write $c=1+y+x(y^{5}+y^{8})$ for this code, which is what we use in Fig. 17.

Due to the structure of Eq. (88), we can find a low-weight cycle basis for $G$ that give low-weight $Z$ checks ( $A_{-1}$ ) of $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ . The cycle basis of $G$ is given by a basis of $\mathrm{ker}(\partial_{1}^{T})\subset\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2l}$ , which has dimension $l+1$ . Taking $\beta=3$ as an example, a natural basis of $\mathrm{ker}(\partial_{1}^{T})$ is

$$ \mathrm{ker}(\partial_{1}^{T})=\mathrm{span}\{\{S_{i}[(1,1,1,0,\cdots,0),(1,0,\cdots,0)]^{T}\}_{i=0}^{l-1}\cup\{[(1,1,\cdots,1),(0,0,\cdots,0)]^{T}\}\}, $$

where $[u,v]$ denotes a vector in $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2l}$ with two blocks $u\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{l}$ and $v\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{l}$ , and $S_{i}$ denotes a cyclic permutation matrix by $i$ in $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{2l\times 2l}$ . The first $l$ basis vectors in Eq. (89) have weight $4$ whereas the last basis vector has a large weight $l$ . Nevertheless, we can reduce the weight of the last basis vector by adding the first $l$ low-weight vectors. For instance, for $l=11$ , we can reduce the last vector to weight $5$ .

Now, we specify how the $X$ checks in $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ are connected to $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ according to $f_{1}$ and $f_{1}^{\prime}$ in Eq. (83), respectively. The way that the ancilla graph $G(V,E)$ is constructed simply gives $f_{1}=\tau^{T}$ , i.e. $f_{1}$ takes a transversal form of $\left(\begin{array}[]{c}I_{l}\\ 0\\ \end{array}\right)$ , where the first $l$ rows are associated with $\mathrm{supp}(\bar{X}_{U,1})$ . Note that when constructing $G$ , we add a unique edge for each $s_{Z}$ of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ that has a nontrivial support on $\mathrm{supp}(\bar{X}_{U,1})$ . As such, we set $f_{0}$ similarly in a transversal form that connects each qubit (associated with an edge) in $A_{0}$ with its corresponding $Z$ check in $Q_{0}$ . So far, the connection between $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ simply follows the standard construction in Ref. [14] since $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ is nothing but the standard ancilla system constructed for measuring $\bar{X}_{U,1}$ of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ . The connection between $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ , on the other hand, leverages the structure that $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ has some components that simply correspond to a repetition code, which exactly matches the structure of $\bar{X}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ and its incident $Z$ checks in $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ . As shown in Fig. 17, by choosing $\bar{X}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ as the bottom boundary of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ , we can construct a graph $G^{\prime}(V^{\prime},E^{\prime})$ , where $V^{\prime}$ with $|V^{\prime}|=d_{c}+d_{s,X}$ are associated with $\mathrm{supp}(\bar{X}_{\mathrm{CS}})$ and $E^{\prime}$ with $|E^{\prime}|=d_{c}+d_{s,X}-1$ are associated with the $Z$ checks of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ that each has weight- $2$ support on $V^{\prime}$ . Since $G^{\prime}$ has takes the form of a repetition code, similar to a subset of the graph $G$ with only checks in the first block $H_{\mathrm{cyc}}(1+z,l)$ of Eq. (88), we can choose $f_{1}^{\prime}$ and $f_{0}^{\prime}$ both in a transversal form that connects pairs of vertices in $V$ and $V^{\prime}$ and pairs of edges in $E$ and $E^{\prime}$ , respectively. We illustrate the above connection of $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ with $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ in Fig. 17.

In the following, we prove that the merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ constructed above has a distance $\geq d_{b}$ if $d_{c}+d_{s,X}\geq d_{b}$ .

#### Definition 25 (Relative Cheeger constant).

Given a check matrix $H\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times n}$ , a subset of column indices $\mathbf{S}\subseteq[n]$ , and an integer $t$ , the relative Cheeger constant $\beta_{t}(H,\mathbf{S})$ is defined as

$$ \beta_{t}(H,\mathbf{S}):=\min_{v\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n},|v|\leq t}\frac{|Hv|}{|v|_{\mathbf{S}}|}. $$

We define $\beta(H,\mathbf{S})$ as $\beta_{t=\infty}(H,\mathbf{S})$ .

#### Lemma 26 (Distance guarantee of the merged code in Def. 24).

Let $d_{X}$ and $d_{Z}$ (resp. $d_{X}^{\prime}$ and $d_{Z}^{\prime}$ ) be the $X$ and $Z$ distance of $\mathcal{Q}$ (resp. $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ ). The $Z$ distance of the merged code $\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}(\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{Q}^{\prime},\mathcal{A})$ in Def. 24 is naturally guaranteed: $\tilde{d}_{Z}\geq d_{Z}+d_{Z}^{\prime}$ . Let $H_{g}:=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\partial_{1}&0\\ f_{1}^{\prime}&H_{x}^{\prime T}\\ \end{array}\right)$ and $\mathbf{C}_{A}$ denotes its first block of columns, the $X$ distance of the merged code satisfies $\tilde{d}_{X}\geq d_{X}$ if

$$ \beta(H_{g},\mathbf{C}_{A})\geq 1. $$

#### Proof.

We first prove the $Z$ distance. Let $v=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}v_{B}\\ v_{A}\\ v_{C}\\ \end{array}\right)$ be a $Z$ operator, where $v_{B}\in Q_{1}$ , $v_{A}\in A_{0}$ , and $v_{C}\in Q_{1}^{\prime}$ , that commutes with the merged $X$ checks, i.e. $\tilde{H}_{X}v=0$ . We have $H_{X}v_{B}=H_{X}^{\prime}v_{C}=0$ . Thus, $v_{B}$ (resp. $v_{C}$ ) has to be either a $Z$ check or a $Z$ logical operator of $\mathcal{Q}$ (resp. $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ ). We now prove that if $v$ is a nontrivial logical operator of the merged code, $v_{B}$ and $v_{C}$ have to take the form of $\bar{Z}\bar{Z}^{\prime}$ for some logical $Z$ operator $\bar{Z}$ of $\mathcal{Q}$ and some logical $Z$ operator $\bar{Z}^{\prime}$ of $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ . We prove this by contradiction. First, assume that both $v_{B}$ and $v_{C}$ are stabilizers, i.e. $v_{B}=H_{Z}^{T}w_{B}$ and $v_{C}=H_{Z}^{\prime T}w_{C}$ for some $w_{B}\in Q_{0}$ and $w_{C}\in Q_{0}^{\prime}$ . From the condition that $\tilde{H}_{X}v=0$ , we have

$$ f_{1}^{T}v_{B}+f_{1}^{\prime T}v_{C}+\partial_{1}^{T}v_{A}=0. $$

From the commutativity of the diagram in Eq. (83), we have $f_{1}^{T}H_{Z}^{T}=\partial_{1}^{T}f_{0}^{T}$ and $f_{1}^{\prime T}H_{Z}^{\prime T}=\partial_{1}^{T}f_{0}^{\prime T}$ . Then, Eq. (92) becomes

$$ \partial_{1}^{T}(f_{0}^{T}w_{B}+f_{0}^{\prime T}w_{C}+v_{A})=0. $$

Thus, $f_{0}^{T}w_{B}+f_{0}^{\prime T}w_{C}+v_{A}\in\mathrm{ker}(\partial_{1}^{T})$ . Since $\mathrm{ker}(\partial_{1}^{T})=\mathrm{im}(\partial_{0}^{T})$ , we have $f_{0}^{T}w_{B}+f_{0}^{\prime T}w_{C}+v_{A}\in\mathrm{ker}(\partial_{1}^{T})=\partial_{0}^{T}w_{A}$ for some $w_{A}\in A_{-1}$ . This leads to $v=\tilde{H}_{Z}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}w_{B}\\ w_{A}\\ w_{C}\\ \end{array}\right)$ , which indicates that $v$ is a $Z$ stabilizer of the merged code, thus contradicting the assumption. Second, assume that either $v_{B}$ or $v_{C}$ is a $Z$ check. Without loss of generality, assume that $v_{B}$ is a $Z$ check of $\mathcal{Q}$ while $v_{C}$ is a $Z$ logical operator of $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ . Let $w_{A}\in\mathrm{ker}(\partial_{1})$ and $s_{X}=\tilde{H}_{X}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ w_{A}\\ 0\\ \end{array}\right)$ be a $X$ check of the merged code. From the condition in Eq. (85), we know that $s_{X}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\bar{X}\\ 0\\ \bar{X}^{\prime}\\ \end{array}\right)$ for some $X$ logical operator $\bar{X}$ of $\mathcal{Q}$ and some $X$ logical operator $\bar{X}^{\prime}$ of $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ . Since $v_{B}=H_{Z}^{T}w_{B}$ for some $w_{B}\in Q_{0}$ , we have $s_{X}^{T}v=\bar{X}^{T}v_{B}+\bar{X}^{\prime T}v_{C}=\bar{X}^{T}H_{Z}^{T}w_{B}+\bar{X}^{\prime T}v_{C}$ = $\bar{X}^{\prime T}v_{C}$ . Since $v_{C}$ is a $Z$ logical operator of $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ , there exists some choice of $s_{X}$ and $\bar{X}^{\prime}$ such that $s_{X}^{T}v=\bar{X}^{\prime T}v_{C}\neq 0$ , which violates the assumption that $v$ is a logical $Z$ operator of the merged code.

Based on the above analysis, both $v_{B}$ and $v_{C}$ have to be a $Z$ logical operator of $Q$ and $Q^{\prime}$ , respectively, which guarantees that $|v|\geq|v_{B}|+|v_{C}|\geq d_{Z}+d_{Z}^{\prime}$ .

Finally, we prove the $X$ distance of the merged code utilizing the condition that $H_{g}$ has a large (relative) Cheeger constant (Eq. (91)). It is easy to check that the logical $X$ operators of the merged code can be represented purely by those of the code $\mathcal{Q}$ , i.e. $\{\bar{X}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ . We now prove that any operator in $\mathrm{span}\{\bar{X}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ cannot be weight reduced below $d_{X}$ by applying the $X$ checks of the merged code. Let $L=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}L_{B}\\ 0\\ 0\\ \end{array}\right)$ be such a merged-code $X$ logical operator, where $L_{B}\in\mathrm{span}\{\bar{X}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}$ . Let $s_{X}=\tilde{H}_{X}^{T}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}w_{B}\\ w_{A}\\ w_{C}\\ \end{array}\right)$ be an arbitrary $X$ check of the merged code. We have $L+s_{X}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}L_{B}+H_{X}^{T}w_{B}+f_{1}w_{A}\\ H_{g}w_{AC}\\ \end{array}\right)$ , where $w_{AC}:=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}w_{A}\\ w_{C}\\ \end{array}\right)$ . Since $f_{1}$ has a maximum row- and column-weight of $1$ , $|f_{1}w_{A}|\leq|w_{A}|$ . Using the relative expansion of $H_{g}$ with respect to $\mathbf{C}_{A}$ , we have $|H_{g}w_{AC}|\geq|w_{A}|$ . Then, $|L+s_{X}|\geq|L_{B}+H_{X}^{T}w_{B}|-|f_{1}w_{A}|+|H_{g}^{T}w_{AC}|\geq|L_{B}+H_{X}^{T}w_{B}|\geq d_{X}$ . ∎

#### Lemma 27 (Distance of the merged color-surface code).

Given a $[[n_{c},1,d_{c}]]$ -color code and a surface code with a $Z$ distance $d_{c}$ and a $X$ distance $d_{s,X}$ , the merged color-surface code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ has a $Z$ distance $d_{c}$ and a $X$ distance $d_{c}+d_{s,X}$ .

#### Proof.

The dual of the color-surface code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ , $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ with a $X$ distance $d_{X}^{\prime}$ and a $Z$ distance $d_{Z}^{\prime}$ , is a merged code in Def. 24 through a repetition code adapter, where $\mathcal{Q}$ is given by the color code and $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ is given by the dual of the surface code. We simply need to prove that $d_{Z}^{\prime}=d_{c}+d_{s,X}$ and $d_{X}^{\prime}\geq d_{c}$ . According to Lemma. 91, we are naturally guaranteed that $d_{Z}^{\prime}\geq d_{c}+d_{s,X}$ , and it remains to show that $H_{g}$ , which is associated with the $X$ checks on the adapter and the surface code, satisfies the large-Cheeger-constant condition in Eq. (91). We now prove this based on the “topological” property of the adapter and the surface code. Let $w=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}w_{A}\\ w_{S}\end{array}\right)$ be a vector on the space of the $X$ checks, where $w_{A}$ and $w_{S}$ are associated with the $X$ checks on the adapter and the surface code, respectively. We have $H_{g}w=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\partial_{1}w_{A}\\ f_{1}^{\prime}w_{A}+H_{x}^{\prime T}w_{S}\end{array}\right)$ . Now, we prove that $|H_{g}w|\geq|f_{1}^{\prime}w_{A}+H_{x}^{\prime T}w_{S}|\geq|w_{A}|$ . As illustrated in Fig. 18, $w_{A}$ is supported on a column of interface $X$ checks and on $|w_{A}|$ rows. $f_{1}^{\prime}w_{A}$ is supported on a column of the surface code data qubits spanning the same set of rows as $w_{A}$ does. Based on the structure of the surface code, applying $H_{x}^{\prime T}w_{S}$ does not reduce the row weight of $f_{1}w_{A}$ , i.e. $f_{1}^{\prime}w_{A}+H_{x}^{\prime T}w_{S}$ always has a nontrivial support on a row $R$ whenever $f_{1}^{\prime}w_{A}$ has support on $R$ . As such, we have $|f_{1}^{\prime}w_{A}+H_{x}^{\prime T}w_{S}|\geq|f_{1}^{\prime}w_{A}|=|w_{A}|$ . Therefore, we have $d^{\prime}_{X}\geq d_{c}$ as the boundary Cheeger constant of $H_{g}$ is larger than $1$ , according to Lemma. 91. ∎

#### Proposition 28 (Distance of the merged color-surface-BB code).

Given $k_{b}$ copies of $[[n_{c},1,d_{c}]]$ color codes and $[[n_{s},1,d_{s,X},d_{s,Z}=d_{c}]]$ thin surface codes and a $[[n_{b},k_{b},d_{c}]]$ BB code, where $d_{c}+d_{s,X}\geq d_{b}$ , the merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ has a distance $\geq d_{b}$ .

According to Lemma 27, each color-surface code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ has a $Z$ distance $d_{cs,Z}=d_{c}$ and a $X$ distance $d_{cs,X}=d_{c}+d_{s,X}\geq d_{b}$ . The color-surface-BB code is a merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}=\tilde{Q}(\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}},\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}^{\otimes k_{b}},\bigotimes_{i=1}^{k_{b}}\mathcal{A}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}})$ defined in Def. 24, where $\mathcal{Q}$ is given by $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ and $\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}$ is given by $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ . According to Lemma 91, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ has a $Z$ distance $\geq d_{b}+d_{\mathrm{cs,Z}}=d_{b}+d_{c}>d_{b}$ as well as a $X$ distance $\geq d_{b}$ if the corresponding $H_{g}$ , which is associated with the $X$ checks of $\otimes_{i=1}^{k_{b}}\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(i)}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ , has a large relative Cheeger constant (see eq. (91)). Since the $k_{b}$ copies of the adapter $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(i)}$ and the color-surface code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ have disjoint support, it suffices to prove the corresponding $H_{g}^{(1)}$ when merging the BB code with only one color code through an adapter $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}^{(1)}$ has a large boundary Cheeger constant. Since $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ has a topological structure, we conjecture that one can find an analytical proof that is analogous to that for Lemma. 27. Here, for simplicity, we simply numerically verified that $\beta(H_{g}^{(1)T},\mathbf{C}_{A})\geq 1$ holds for all the BB codes listed in Table I of the main text.

Note that in practice, we might choose a smaller ancillary surface code such that the $X$ distance of the merged color-surface code, $d_{c}+d_{s,X}$ , is smaller than $d_{b}$ . In this case, the distance of the merged color-surface-BB code, will be determined by $d_{c}+d_{s,X}$ . For instance, to minimize the overall logical error rates, we choose $d_{c}+d_{s,X}=7$ for the $[[66,6,8]]$ -BB code, which will result in a merged code with distance $7$ .

### S5.2 Code-merging protocol

In Alg 1, we present a code deformation protocol that starts with $k_{b}$ copies of color codes, $\mathcal{Q}_{C}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ , and ends in one merged color-surface-BB code, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ . At the high level, the protocol is analogous to the growth of surface codes [54, 97] and it grows the logical operators of the small color code in two steps: (i) grow the $X$ logical operators to weight $d_{c}+d_{s,X}\geq d_{b}$ by merging with thin surface codes (ii) grow the $Z$ logical operators to weight $\geq d_{c}+d_{b}$ by merging with the BB code.

```
Input : $k_{b}$ copies of $[[n_{c},1,d_{c}]]$ -color code $Q_{C}$ .
Output : A merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ encoding the same information as that in $\mathcal{Q}_{C}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ .
1 Construct the merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ as $\tilde{Q}(Q_{\mathrm{BB}},Q_{\mathrm{CS}}^{\otimes k_{b}},\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}})$ according to Def. 24, where $Q_{\mathrm{CS}}$ is constructed as $\tilde{Q}(\mathcal{Q}_{C},\mathcal{Q}_{S},\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{C-S}})$ . See Sec. S5.1 for the details of the construction.
2 Prepare the data qubits of the surface codes $\mathcal{Q}_{S}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ and the color-surface adapters $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{C-S}}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ in $\ket{+}$ states and measure the stabilizers of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ for one round.
3 Prepare the data qubits of the BB code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ and the color-surface-BB adapter $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{CS-BB}}$ in $\ket{0}$ states and measure the stabilizers of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ for $t_{m}$ rounds.
4 Restart the protocol when certain detectors (see Fig. 19 and the text for details) are triggered.
5 Calculate soft information (complementary gap) of the decoder correction for the merged code and restart when it is unreliable.
```

We illustrate the stabilizer measurements and the detectors of the code merging protocol in Alg. 1 in Fig. 19. Counting the round of stabilizer measurements on the merged color-surface code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ in the step 2 of Alg. 1 as the zero-th code cycle, the protocol establishes the full set of deterministic $X$ stabilizers (resp. $Z$ stabilizers) on the merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ and gains sufficiently large $Z$ distance (resp. $X$ distance) at the second (first) code cycle. We need to post-select on the detectors before this stage, where the space distance of the protocol is still small, to prevent logical errors from low-weight space-like faults. In addition, we also post-select on part of the detectors after reaching the full space distance to prevent logical errors from the combination of space-like and time-like errors. As shown in Fig. 19(a) and (b), respectively, we post-select on the $X$ and $Z$ detectors only on the merged color-surface codes $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ and the color codes $\mathcal{Q}_{C}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ , starting from the zero-th code cycle to up to $\tau_{X}$ and $\tau_{Z}$ code cycles on the merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ , respectively. We provide the choice of $\tau_{X}$ and $\tau_{Z}$ that balances the space-like logical error rates and the success rate of the protocol in Table 2. Finally, we perform light post-selection on the merged code based on the soft information (aka complimentary gap [27]) quantifying the reliability of the decoder corrections to further reduce the error rates of the final $\ket{T}$ states. See Methods in Ref. [98] for obtaining such soft information using an integer-programming decoder and upcoming work [99] for doing so with the BP+OSD decoder (used in this work).

We probe the space-like logical error rates and the time-like logical error rates of the code merging protocol of Alg. 1 separately using the memory experiment and the stability experiment [92], respectively. For the memory experiment, we initialize the data qubits of the $k_{b}$ color codes $\mathcal{Q}_{C}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ in $\ket{+}$ (resp. $\ket{0}$ ) states, simulate the merging protocol in Alg. 1, and measure the data qubits of the final merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ in the $X$ (resp. $Z$ ) basis, and estimate the logical $Z$ (resp. $X$ ) error rate by checking if values of the logical $X$ (resp. $Z$ ) operators of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ are all $+1$ . We refer to the logical failure probability (LFP) as the probability that any of the logical operators are measured in $-1$ and approximately estimate the logical failure rate per logical qubit as $\mathrm{LFR}=\mathrm{LFP}/k_{b}$ . We plot the logical $Z$ and $X$ error rate versus the physical error rate in Fig. 20(a)-(b).

For the stability experiment, we utilize the redundancy of the $X$ checks $H_{X}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r\times n}$ of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ , i.e. $\mathrm{ker}(H_{X}^{T})\neq 0$ . In the code-merging protocol in Alg. 1, the $X$ syndromes $\{s_{X}(t)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r}\}_{t=1}^{t_{m}}$ on the merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ for different code cycles $t$ are non-deterministic (but should be the same across different cycles) in the absence of errors. However, due to the redundancy of $H_{X}$ , there are certain combinations of the syndromes at a given round, i.e. $\mathbf{S}=\{a^{T}s_{X}(t)\mid a\in\mathrm{ker}(H_{X}^{T})\}$ , that should be deterministically $+1$ . Denote the time-like logical failure probability $\mathrm{LFP}^{T}$ as the probability that any element in $\mathbf{S}$ takes a $-1$ value after the error correction, we characterize the time-like logical error rate per logical qubit as $p^{T}_{L}=\mathrm{LFP}^{T}/k_{b}$ . These time-like logical failures characterize the failures of obtaining the correct $X$ stabilizer frame of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ in Alg. 1 when growing the logical $Z$ operators by appending the block of qubits of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ in the $\ket{0}$ states during the step 3. Note that we only need to reliably obtain the $X$ checks by repeating multiple code cycles when considering the teleportation circuit in Fig. 6(c) of the main text since the merging protocol is followed by transversal $Z$ measurements. We plot the time-like logical failure rate $p_{L}^{T}$ of the merged $[[216,6,5]]$ code and the $[[324,6,7]]$ code for different choices of $t_{m}$ in Fig. 20(c).

Finally, we estimate the fidelity and the space-time costs for the final $\ket{T}$ states hosted in the $[[324,6,7]]$ merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ . Since the initial cultivation steps on the $d=3$ color codes [27] has an negligible error rates and space-time costs compared to our code-merging protocol here, we simply assume that we start from $k_{b}=6$ copies of perfect $\ket{T}$ states encoded in the color codes. Let $N_{\mathrm{CSBB}}=648$ denote the total number of qubits for $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ , which includes both the data qubits and the ancilla qubits. We estimate the fidelity of the final $\ket{T}$ states by summing up the space-like logical error rates (in Fig. 20(a)-(b)) and the time-like logical error rates (Fig. 20(c)), $p_{L}(\ket{T})\approx p_{L}^{X}+p_{L}^{Z}+p_{L}^{T}\approx 2\times 10^{-5}$ (see Table 2). Clearly, the space-time costs are dominated by the $t_{m}$ code cycles (including retries) spent on the merged $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ code. The post-selection is primarily applied on the first $\tau_{X}=2$ code cycles. We assume that we restart the protocol whenever we detect any nontrivial syndromes after each of the $\tau_{X}$ code cycles. Let $\eta=\eta_{Z}\eta_{X}=0.65$ be the success rate per cycle. It then takes on average $t_{0}=(1+\eta)/\eta^{2}\approx 3.9$ cycles to complete the first two (post-selected) code cycles. The total number of code cycles for the entire merging protocol is then roughly given by $T\approx(t_{0}+t_{m}-2)/(\eta_{X}^{s}\eta_{Z}^{s})\approx 8$ . The space-time cost (per kept $\ket{T}$ state) is then given by $W(\ket{T})\approx N_{\mathrm{CSBB}}*T/6\approx 860\ \mathrm{qubit*cycles}$ .

### S5.3 Homomorphic CNOT

Here, we prove that the block of the cultivated magic states $\overline{\ket{T}}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ in the merged code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ can be used to teleport parallel $\bar{T}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ gates on a data BB code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ (see Fig.5(c) of the main text) by implementing a homomorphic CNOT between $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ . Specifically, we prove in Proposition 29 that pairs of physical CNOTs that each couples a data qubit of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ and the corresponding data qubit of the BB component of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ (see the gray patch in Fig. 17) implement parallel logical $\mathrm{CNOT}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ between pairs of logical qubits of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ . Moreover, this homomorphic CNOT is trivially fault-tolerant since it only involves transversal physical CNOTs that do not spread errors within a code block.

#### Proposition 29 (Homomorphic CNOT from the merged code to the BB code).

The $n_{b}$ pairs of physical CNOTs that are each controlled by a data qubit of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ and targeting the corresponding data qubit of the BB component of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ implement parallel logical CNOTs, $\overline{\mathrm{CNOT}}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ , controlled by $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ and targeting $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ .
