### S5.4 Logical translation

We implement the logical translation gadget for a BB code by leveraging the translational automorphism of the constructed BB codes. As detailed in the main text, the $k_{b}$ logical qubits of a $[[n_{b},k_{b},d_{b}]]$ - $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ are distributed into two blocks with indices $\{1,2,\cdots,k_{b}/2\}$ and $\{k_{b}/2+1,\cdots,k_{b}\}$ , which can be cyclically permuted within each block using physical permutations. To complete a joint cyclic permutation on $k_{b}$ logical qubits, we compose the above automorphism gate with an extra swap between the qubits indexed by $1$ and $k_{b}/2+1$ . Such an extra swap could be implemented using standard surgery-based approaches [43] by, e.g. teleporting the targeted pair of logical qubits to two $[[n_{s},1,d_{s}\geq d_{b}]]$ surface codes and then swapping the two surface codes, analogous to how an addressable logical CNOT can be performed on any qLDPC code using a toric-code ancilla [43]. Note that as we only need to perform a single swap operation using a single ancilla surgery system, the overheads and the logical error rates of this targeted swap operation will both be much lower than those of the parallel magic-state cultivation procedure, which involves $k_{b}$ surgery systems.

### S5.5 Clifford fixups

Here, we describe how to implement the Clifford fixups on the data BB code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ when teleporting global $T$ gates in Fig. 6(c) of the main text, which is also copied here in Fig. 21(a).

Depending on the $Z$ measurement outcomes on the merged color-surface-BB code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ , we need to apply some addressable $S$ gates, denoted by $\vec{S}$ , on $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ . We implement $\vec{S}$ using the circuit in Fig. 21(b): (1) initialize an ancilla code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}^{\prime}$ (identical to $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ ) in the $Z$ basis, (2) resetting a subset (depending on $\vec{S}$ ) of the $k_{b}$ logical qubits of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}^{\prime}$ to $+$ states by doing a set of logical $X$ measurements using surgery systems (indicated by the orange bars in Fig. 21(b)(c)), (3) apply a transversal CNOT between $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}^{\prime}$ , (4) apply transversal $S$ gates on $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}^{\prime}$ , (5) transversally measure $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}^{\prime}$ in the $X$ basis, (6) apply feedback addressable Pauli $Z$ correction on $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ . As shown in Fig. 21(c), the surgery system for performing the selective logical $X$ measurements in step (2) is the same as the adapters that are used to merge the BB code with the color codes. For instance, a surgery system for measuring the $X$ logical operator of the first logical qubit of the “U” block of $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}^{\prime}$ is shown in Fig. 21(c), which is the same as the orange strip in Fig. 17. Since the transversal $Z$ measurements on $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ in Fig. 21(a) will be random, we only need about $k_{b}/2$ surgery systems on average. As such, the space-time cost of the $S$ fixups will be much smaller than the global $T$ gates (Fig. 21(b) versus Fig. 21(a)).

### S5.6 Resource estimates

Finally, we estimate the logical error rates and space–time costs of implementing a parallel layer of two-qubit rotations—the key subroutine for simulating the lattice dynamics in Fig. 6(c) of the main text—using the BB-code–based protocols introduced in this section, assuming a physical error rate of $10^{-3}$ . We benchmark these results against (i) state-of-the-art surface-code protocols and (ii) a BB-code protocol that implements the same task via sequential coupling to a cultivated surface-code magic-state factory [56], which we refer to as the low-rate BB protocol.

The three protocols are illustrated in Fig. 22. Each implements $k_{b}$ parallel $ZZ(\theta)$ rotations between two blocks of $k_{b}$ logical qubits, each encoded in a $k_{b}$ -logical-qubit data code. The operation is realized by sandwiching a global $Z(\theta)^{\otimes k_{b}}$ rotation on one block between two transversal inter-block CNOTs. The global $Z(\theta)^{\otimes k_{b}}$ rotations are synthesized from sequences of global $H^{\otimes k_{b}}$ , $S^{\otimes k_{b}}$ , and $T^{\otimes k_{b}}$ gates. The $T$ gates, in turn, are implemented by coupling the data code to a factory code that hosts cultivated high-fidelity $\ket{T}$ states. Below we detail the implementation for each protocol.

Surface-code protocol. As shown in Fig. 22(a), the two data codes are chosen as $k_{b}$ copies of a rotated $[[81,1,d_{S}=9]]$ surface code $\mathcal{Q}_{S}$ , and the factory code consists of $k_{b}$ copies of a distance- $d_{\mathrm{GCS}}=15$ grafted color-surface code[27, 56], denoted $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{GCS}}$ . Using Pauli-based computation [101], the global $H^{\otimes k_{b}}$ and $S^{\otimes k_{b}}$ are absorbed into Clifford transformations, so that the global $T^{\otimes k_{b}}$ gets transformed to parallel Pauli rotations $P(\pi/8)$ ( $P\in{X,Y,Z}$ ). Each such rotation is implemented by parallel $P\otimes Z$ joint Pauli-product measurements between $\mathcal{Q}_{S}$ and $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{GCS}}$ . These measurements can be carried out in $d_{S}$ code cycles using $k_{b}$ copies of a surface-to-surface adapter $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{S-S}}$ (the orange strip in Fig.22(a)). $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{S-S}}$ simply takes a form of a $d_{\mathrm{GCS}}$ -bit repetition code. We denote by $t_{\mathrm{cul,S}}$ the expected number of code cycles to obtain the cultivated $\ket{T}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ states in $\mathcal{Q}{\mathrm{GCS}}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ . We adopt a rough estimate of $t{\mathrm{cul,S}}=10$ , consistent with the $\sim 4000$ qubit $\times$ cycle volume required for a $\ket{T}$ state error rate of $3\times 10^{-5}$ [27]. These estimates are admittedly coarse and could be further optimized. However, $t_{\mathrm{cul,S}}=10$ should be regarded as optimistic, especially given the challenge of performing many (probabilistic) parallel cultivations.

Low-rate BB protocol. Fig. 22(b) depicts the analogous construction using BB codes. Each data block is now a $[[66,6,8]]$ BB code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ (see Table I in the main text). The key difference is that the global $T^{\otimes k_{b}}$ is implemented sequentially. Specifically, each logical qubit in $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ is coupled in turn to a single $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{GCS}}$ factory code via a joint Pauli product measurement, using a BB–surface adapter $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{S-BB}}$ in $d_{b}$ code cycles. For simplicity, we assume $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{S-BB}}$ is identical to the BB–color-surface adapter $\mathcal{A}{\mathrm{CS-BB}}$ defined in Sec.S5.1, although this assumption is optimistic since $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{GCS}}$ is larger than $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{CS}}$ . Note that such a sequential BB protocol, adopted in Ref. [56], is necessary when, for instance, the data BB code $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ , e.g. the Gross code in Ref. [11], does not have a disjoint logical-operator basis, in which case parallel surgeries are challenging.

High-rate BB protocol. Finally, Fig. 22(c) illustrates the fully parallel BB-code protocol introduced in this work. Here the data blocks are again encoded in $\mathcal{Q}{\mathrm{BB}}=[[66,6,8]]$ , but the factory consists of a $[[324,6,7]]$ color-surface-BB code $\mathcal{Q}{\mathrm{CSBB}}$ , which prepares $\ket{T}^{\otimes k_{b}}$ in an expected $t_{\mathrm{cul,BB}}\approx 8$ code cycles. These $\ket{T}$ states are then used to teleport the global $T^{\otimes k_{b}}$ on one $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{BB}}$ block via the homomorphic transversal CNOT (Sec.S5.3), followed by feedback $S$ gates applied in $d_{b}$ logical cycles (Sec.S5.5). The global $H^{\otimes k_{b}}$ and $S^{\otimes k_{b}}$ gates can be applied transversally in $O(1)$ logical cycles using correlated decoding[102, 63]. These Clifford operations can be executed concurrently with the factory’s $\ket{T}$ state preparation, incurring no additional code-cycle overhead.

For a small angle such as $\theta=\pi/64$ , we can synthesize $Z(\theta)$ using $n_{T}=11$ $T/T^{\dagger}$ gates and $13$ $H$ and $S/S^{\dagger}$ gates with a synthesis error $\approx 8\times 10^{-5}$ . To simulate a $R$ by $2k_{b}$ lattice with $K=R\times(2k_{b})$ algorithm logical qubits, the total footprint per algorithm qubit for the three protocols are:

- 1. $N_{\mathrm{surface}}/K=R\times k_{b}\times(2N_{S}+N_{\mathrm{GCS}}+N_{A,\mathrm{S-S}})/K\approx 403$ .

- 2. $N_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}/K=R\times(2N_{\mathrm{BB}}+N_{\mathrm{GCS}}+N_{A,\mathrm{S-BB}})/K\approx 64$ .

- 3. $N_{\mathrm{BB,high-rate}}/K=R\times(2N_{\mathrm{BB}}+N_{\mathrm{CSBB}})/K\approx 76$ .

The total number of code cycles are dominated by the number of global $T$ layers $n_{T}$ multiplied by the code cycles per $T$ layer:

- 1. $t_{\mathrm{surface}}\approx n_{T}\times(t_{\mathrm{cul,S}}+d_{S})=209$ .

- 2. $t_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}\approx n_{T}\times k_{b}\times(t_{\mathrm{cul},S}+d_{b}-1)=1122$ .

- 3. $t_{\mathrm{BB,high-rate}}\approx n_{T}\times(t_{\mathrm{cul,BB}}+d_{b}-1)=165$ .

Note that the extra factor $k_{b}$ contributing to $t_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}$ arises from the fact that each layer of global $T^{\otimes k_{b}}$ gates are injected sequentially. Here, we have used $d_{b}-1$ instead of $d_{b}$ for $t_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{BB,high-rate}}$ as $d_{b}=8$ is even for the $[[66,6,8]]$ BB code.

The total physical circuit depth is estimated by multiplying the number of code cycles by the physical depth per cycle— $\tau_{\mathrm{cul,S}}$ for the surface-code and low-rate BB protocols, and $\tau_{\mathrm{cul,BB}}$ for the high-rate BB protocol:

- 1. $T_{\mathrm{surface}}\approx t_{\mathrm{surface}}\times\tau_{\mathrm{cul},S}$ = 1672.

- 2. $T_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}\approx t_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}\times\tau_{\mathrm{cul},S}=8976$ .

- 3. $T_{\mathrm{BB,high-rate}}\approx t_{\mathrm{BB,high-rate}}\times\tau_{\mathrm{{cul},BB}}=2310$ .

Note that we have used $\tau_{\mathrm{cul,BB}}=14$ by assuming a depth-optimal syndrome extraction circuit for the merged CSBB code with a stabilizer weight $12$ [103]. We expect that the logical error rates for a more compact circuit would be comparable to the coloration circuit that we use in the current simulations under the error model that excludes idling errors.

We then estimate the total space-time volumes per logical qubit by multiplying the footprints per logical qubit by the physical circuit depth:

- 1. $W_{\mathrm{surface}}/K\approx N_{\mathrm{surface}}/K\times T_{\mathrm{surface}}\approx 6.7\times 10^{5}$ .

- 2. $W_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}/K\approx N_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}/K\times T_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}\approx 5.7\times 10^{5}$ .

- 3. $W_{\mathrm{BB,high-rate}}/K\approx N_{\mathrm{BB,high-rate}}/K\times T_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}=\approx 1.8\times 10^{5}$ .

Finally, we estimate the logical error rate per logical qubit. Since the relevant logical operations across the different codes and protocols all exhibit a comparable error rate per cycle, $p_{L,0}\approx 4\times 10^{-6}$ , we can approximate the total logical error per qubit for each layer of parallel two-qubit rotations as:

- 1. $p_{L}(\mathrm{surface})/K\approx p_{L,0}\times t_{\mathrm{surface}}\approx 8\times 10^{-4}$ .

- 2. $p_{L}(\mathrm{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}})/K\approx p_{L,0}\times t_{\mathrm{BB,low-rate}}\approx 4\times 10^{-3}$ .

- 3. $p_{L}({\mathrm{BB,high-rate}})/K\approx p_{L,0}\times t_{\mathrm{BB,high-rate}}\approx 7\times 10^{-4}$ .
